en: The Āṅgirasasmṛti [says]: "O twice-born ones, [he approached] the ancient Aṅgiras, the sage Āṅgirasa himself, who was like the purifying fire."
"Speak the Dharma in its entirety," they said to him, having prostrated before him.
Then, out of affection for them, he proclaimed: "Listen!
I shall declare all those supreme Vedic dharmas that lead to liberation. (1.2)
Dharma is said to be that which is enjoined by the Vedic injunction; anything other than that is so called only figuratively.
That injunction, consisting of the optative suffix and so forth, should be known as the bestower of liberation when impelled by the Śruti.

That alone is the injunction (codanā), characterized by the optative, imperative, and gerundive suffixes as declared in the Śruti, and not any other; it is that which is enjoined in the Purāṇas and the Smṛtis.
One who is learned in the Vedas should not perform rites prescribed in the Purāṇas; he should not carry out rituals according to the rules stated in the Purāṇas.
He should perform all rites using only those mantras that are declared in the Vedas. Angiras 1.5.
Merely by the recitation of mantras spoken in the Purāṇas during the midst of a ritual act, the Vedic rite would perish; therefore, one should not practice in that manner.
One should act accordingly even when these [rites] mentioned in the Purāṇas as well as those worldly ones are present;
for in the absence of specific mantras, the *vyāhṛtis* are prescribed everywhere— it is said that the *vyāhṛtis* are indeed the mantras in all cases where mantras are absent.

In the lineage, others [hold that] those respective mantras are possible for those various rites either through an indicative mark (liṅga), from the meaning (artha), or due to the absence of contradiction. Ang_1.8.
Wherever no expiation is seen anywhere at all,
for that [offense], this divine and most excellent expiation has indeed been declared.
The sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*) are meritorious; this *ṛc* belongs to Viṣṇu and is auspicious.
It pacifies all sins and bestows the very objects one has contemplated.
In the past, Viṣṇu determined that for the purpose of performing expiatory rites,
there is no mantra equal to the Vyāhṛtis, and no recitation equal to the Vyāhṛtis.
There is no sacred ford equal to the *vyāhṛtis*, no austerity equal to the *vyāhṛtis*,
no sacrifice equal to the *vyāhṛtis*, and no ritual acts equal to the *vyāhṛtis*.
Therefore, they are prescribed everywhere solely for the purpose of expiation.
Therefore, [this applies] to all Vedic and worldly activities without exception.
In the total non-occurrence of negligence and in the intentional abandonment thereof,
for both the ignorant and the wise, the saving stars are supreme purifiers.

The Vyāhṛtis are the rescuers; they are joined with the Ṛgveda verses. Furthermore, in the case of the omission of rites such as the birth ceremony (jātakarman), or in the non-performance of a rite, the Vyāhṛtis are prescribed for the [omission] of the birth and naming ceremonies.

Likewise, it is taught that the rites known as Nāmakarman (the naming ceremony) and Annaprāśana (the first feeding of solid food), as well as Caula (the tonsure ceremony), must be accomplished within a single day; otherwise, there are consequences. Ang_1.16 //

Those supreme *vyāhṛtis* which are traditionally held to be accomplished in two days, after which the *mauñjī* (girdle of muñja grass) should be performed; likewise, if the *mauñjī* is not performed, [the following applies].
During the primary period, from the tenth [day] onwards up until the sixteenth year, there are [intervals of] three,
four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and so forth days.
The nights have been described for him; the recitation of that [mantra] is his atonement.
But what [atonement] is there for other actions for which no atonement exists?
These have been declared by the virtuous who constantly proclaim the Vedas;
having recited these divine *vyāhṛtis*, they serve solely for the purpose of expiation. (1.20)
[Once they are] purified, one should then immediately undertake those respective actions;
for one who possesses mere faith, there is a continuous undertaking and commencement of maturation. Ang_1.21 //
Indeed, for him there will arise no specific intention at all.

If, after the cooking for the *śrāddha*, impurity (*āśauca*) should occur due to fate—whether it be birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) during the performance—[the following applies].* Ang_1.22 *Note: This sentence fragment indicates that the ritual proceeds as planned despite the interruption.
In performing that rite, however, nothing shall be an obstacle for them;
therefore, first of all, having bathed properly with the appropriate mantras for the sake of that ritual, [one should proceed].

Then one should perform that ritual action; for as long as they are engaged in it, there is no period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) for them. At the time of performing the rite, that impurity indeed dissolves immediately.
Furthermore, once the rite has been performed, that [impurity] arises again by itself;

if death should occur in that same lineage after the commencement of cooking for a funeral feast (śrāddha), or if a corpse should fall when the commencement of cooking for the feast has already taken place. Ang_1.25.
Even if death should occur on that street before the commencement of the cooking, the śrāddha performed by him on that street would not be defiled; rather,
prior to the commencement of the cooking, its occurrence on that street would serve as an obstacle to the śrāddha.

If a corpse has fallen on the street, but not after the commencement of the cooking process, and if impurity (sūtaka) should occur in the midst of that which has already been undertaken; [then there is no obstacle]. Ang_1.27.
For even if it has arrived, it will not be prevented by him;
therefore, one should likewise perform the śrāddha rite when it has begun, even during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka). Ang_1.28.
The entire process of pacification (ātarpaṇa), beginning from the commencement of the cooking according to the prescribed rite,
as well as the Śrāddha following the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Iṣṭi, and Paśubandha sacrifices,
constitutes a single Śrāddha that serves as a substitute for all Vratas and Kṛcchra penances. (Anga 1.29)
For him as well, there is the turn of sacrifice: the full-moon rite and the new-moon rite;
on that very day, he performs the full-moon, the new-moon, and the animal sacrifice.

Having first completed the *samāgata* and *samāpya* rites, one should subsequently perform the *śrāddha*; for by performing the sacrifice on the day prescribed for ancestral rites (*pitṛkriyā*), all [obligations] are fulfilled. (Ang 1.31)
The Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas in their entirety—
all the ancestors (pitṛs) and all the grandfathers (pitāmahas)— are likewise of that same nature.
May all the great-grandfathers indeed be eternally satisfied;
through the attainment of initiation, their satisfaction shall be most abundant.
For one who has entered the midst of the Great Initiation (mahādīkṣā), the annual śrāddha and the monthly śrāddha for that month shall not take place;
even the annual śrāddha for one’s parents is not prescribed, nor that for paternal uncles and others. (Anga 1.34)
That which has entered the midst of the great initiation will indeed have passed away;
for one who has undergone the great initiation, is it not true that the ritual performance occurs at its conclusion?
Those great initiations should be known as lasting twenty-four days and more.
Among those [initiations], there are three that consist of fewer than six days, such as three or six days and so forth, occurring within the Kharva initiation.

Those [syllables] should be known as being of the nature of *kharva*; the paternal [syllable] situated in their midst, or whatever else is at its end, should be performed; anything other than that is swallowed by them.

When there is an increase in initiation, even if a ritual action has already been performed in the great initiations during the sacrificial sessions (satras), it should not be said that "it need not be done" in any way whatsoever when there is an increase in initiation. (Ang. 1.38)

Even if that śrāddha has already been performed, if by the power of destiny it becomes impossible, one should perform it at the very end of that period; for when else could it be done? (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.39)
If, through the conjunction of destiny, the magnitude of the expansion of consciousness has been attained,
then at its conclusion, through contact with another cause, that which was done and undone [is resolved].
They say that for those who die during the period of initiation (*dīkṣā*), no consecration (*saṃskāra*) should be performed; rather, it becomes a funeral rite (*śrāddha*).
One should neither perform the consecration nor even look upon those who have died during initiation; should one nevertheless perform it, it constitutes a transgression.
Thus has the superiority of Vedic action been established by the illustrious knowers of Brahman, who understand dharma and perceive reality.
It excels even over difficult penances such as acts of charity, pilgrimage sites, and vows;
for the Vedic rite is great, and from it the Veda itself originates.
Being pure, one should perform Vedic rites, not while impure;
for from impurity, the state of being unfit for Brahmins will arise.
Regarding the impurity of childbirth and the state of untouchability: during the impurity of childbirth or the impurity following death, one should not perform Vedic rites.
Untouchability does not apply in the case of childbirth, but it certainly exists during the [other] impurity. (Angiras 1.45)
Upon the death of either of the two great gurus, one should observe a fast;
it is the consensus of all that eating for a day and night constitutes a loss of merit.
Eating at an improper time during a period of impurity caused by death or birth is not permitted;
however, one should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) for those two periods mentally, using only the mantras.
If, while one is already in a state of impurity (āśauca) due to a collective impurity, there occurs again an impurity caused by the death of one, two, three, four, or eight women; 1.48.

There is no direct liberation from food; that [liberation] occurs through the twilight rite performed in water. In the event of constant impurity, those who dwell in the village where hundreds of kinsmen have passed away are perpetually afflicted by sin.
If, at the end of one period of impurity, another period of impurity occurs immediately thereafter, he should wait for a year;
then, having carefully abandoned that village with due respect, he may proceed. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.50)

It is the established rule that the *śrāddha* for one's parents must be performed immediately even when in another country, provided that no obstacle to the *śrāddha* arises through a traditional succession [of impediments]. (Anga 1.51)
Then, having observed for a year, he should immediately depart for another country,
provided that no obstacle to the śrāddha arises at that time.
One should perform the *śrāddha* at that very time while wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*),
provided that one has been simultaneously affected by all three types of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).
Or, after the period of impurity has passed, he should wear the sacrificial thread;
for one who is devoid of the sacrificial thread is unfit for all ritual acts. (Angiras 1.54)
In the absence of that [monastic] robe, one wears either cotton or wool according to the prescribed rule;
no mantra is recited in that regard.
The mantra would be like the sūtra itself, yet devoid of a crest;
if it were one whose crest is severed by an enemy, then one who wears it on the ear while striving for purity would likewise have his crest severed by an enemy instantly. (Ang_1.56)

If the middle part is severed, he becomes pure through the performance of the *prājāpatya* penance followed by the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*); of this there is no doubt. (Ang_1.57) [009] In the case of a severance in the middle.
When the topknot is severed in the middle, it is purified by the Prājāpatya rite;
likewise when the crest-lock is destroyed by disease or the like, or when the entire lock is lost due to illness, or even in times of great distress.
If, however, death occurs by fire against one's will, there must indeed be a re-consecration after ascending the funeral pyre;
one should not perform it prior to that.
In accordance with the prescribed rule, one should indeed wear the hair from a cow's tail as long as she does not become incapacitated by old age or disease.
If, beyond seventy [years], her body is covered with hair— whether on the front,
the back, the sides, or all around— due to the growth of such hairs; // Ang_1.61 //
The topknot (śikhā) must be maintained with effort; if it is not, then nothing at all is accomplished.
This is true even in a place that is entirely empty, let alone elsewhere.
One should wear those hairs in this manner specifically to indicate one's status as a Brahmin;
otherwise, it would not be so. Therefore, one should practice accordingly.
Thus, when eight years have passed, he should enter the third stage of life;
for the topknot and the pair of sacred threads are the very root of Brahminhood.
By whatever means one might wear a topknot and a sacred thread, if the cutting of the topknot should occur five times at the hands of enemies, [one must perform the rite]. (1.65)
His Brahminhood would be lost even through a rite of re-consecration; likewise,
if an obstacle to the śrāddha occurs— such as sexual union with a woman or when an obstacle to the śrāddha arises due to constant impurity from birth or death.
At that time, one should not approach a woman for sexual intercourse without having first performed the *śrāddha* ceremony;
if a fetus has been conceived at that time, one must perform the penance for the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā-vrata*).
Then, in the event of a single instance of union, one should perform three *prājāpatya* penances;
and from repeated intercourse, one should also perform the *āgneya* sacrifice.
Furthermore, the initiatory rite for him was enjoined by the exponents of the Veda:
he who had entered the body of another [should perform it] with his own wife through that very form.
Having entered that [family], one should not consort with them; nor should one consort with their women.
If one were to perform such an action, both that family and your own family would be ruined.

He would cause himself to fall into the terrible hell named Raurava, should the ancestral offering (śrāddha) intended for the three ancestors ever fail, or if the previous oblation (havis) should somehow perish. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.71)
Then, having again prepared that [oblation] and offered it with the *prāṇa* and other [vital airs],
one completes the rite with the remainder of that [caru] after thirty-two oblations.
Regarding that *śrāddha* intended for the three ancestors, its commencement and conclusion should take place in the afternoon;
indeed, the food should be cooked on the very same day at midday.

Because it is cooked separately, its consumption occurs at a second [time]; in that case, there is no such [simultaneous] consumption for the Brahmins; there would be merely their eating, and one should perform this while they are looking on.
Then, at the commencement of the anniversary of the death, the ritual procedure is performed;
taking all the remnants, one should offer nine funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Likewise, in the ritual for the threefold application, one should cause [the disciple] to consume the remainder;
thereafter, when there is great fear, one should provide a profuse meal with care.
If the bride becomes menstruating before the oblation of parched grain (lājāhoma), or if she becomes menstruating prior to that oblation of parched grain,
[the rite should be performed] according to the rule with a hundred jars of water while reciting the mantra "haviṣmatī."
Having bathed [the image] according to the ritual procedure and clothed it with two garments,
one should bow down with effort twice while offering a pair of oblations.
Then, having established a separate fire, one should offer consecrated ghee;
thereafter, the ritual procedure (tantra) should be performed until the dismissal of the Brahmins.
Having loosened the girdle, he should cast it far away from that wife;
thereafter, immediately after she has bathed on the fourth day.
One should perform the rites of carrying [the water] and so forth according to the prescribed rule;
for both of them, the milk-vow (payovrata) must then be observed constantly according to the rule.
Then the domestic fire-oblation (aupāsana-homa) should take place; however, that opinion holds that it occurs from the commencement [of the rite].
If it is after the parched-grain oblation (lāja-homa), then it is after that; if it is after her bath, then it is after that bath. Ang_1.82. [012]
But prior to the final oblation, having silently— without reciting mantras—
given two garments to her and covered her with them, thereafter...
Then, on the third day having passed and on the fourth day,
during the second watch of the day, with vessels of gold consecrated by mantras, [he bathed him].
Having caused the consecration to be performed, one should carry out the remaining rites. However,
if the *aupāsana* fire has not been established, then on the second day—
if indeed on the second day while the *aupāsana* has not been established— Ang_1.85.
Then, while she was in her menses, he gave her another pair of garments silently, without the recitation of mantras, by sprinkling them with the sacrificial oblation.
Having covered it with those two [cloths], one should thereafter perform the consecration on the fourth day with a thousand water-pots accompanied by mantras.
With the five products of the cow, white sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and all kinds of grain,
one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *gāyatrī*.
If one performs one thousand and eight oblations with the *Āyuṣya-sūkta*, using either sacrificial porridge (*caru*) or parched grain (*lāja*), it is the supreme remover of all defects.
Having completed the remainder of the *homa*, one should then complete the remainder of the ritual;
thereafter, one attains purification solely from that action.
Then, on the fifth day thereafter, having established the domestic fire (*aupāsana*),
he should unite with her for the sake of conception according to the ritual procedure for impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) after one month.

Because of the mutual conflict between that house, field, and mind, and because the rites of the deceased have been suppressed, there is birth-impurity resulting from the completion of those [rites]. (Ang_1.92)
For those who have ceased their activities as *preta*s with the desire to seize that property,
until the completion of that [act], it shall be considered *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) for them.

During a period of impurity, they shall not perform obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and other rites— including their completion— as well as auspicious acts; likewise, they shall not perform the Vedic study sacrifice (brahmayajña) and other such rites that are obligatory, occasional, or performed for specific desires.
When the rites for the deceased obstruct [other duties], one should not engage in Vedic recitation, nor perform fire oblations, nor enter an assembly;
one should perform the twilight devotions mentally and should not consume savory foods.
If one should perform those [rites] out of delusion, that preta will not tolerate it;
he will surely utter a terrible curse. Therefore, one must avoid obstructing those duties.
One should not even conceive of it in the mind; that is proclaimed to be a Caṇḍāla.
For such a deed is terrible and wicked; one should never perform such a thing.

In the Kali age, one should not practice excessive injustice and the like; even in the Kali age, one should neither commit nor cause others to commit extreme treachery, extreme cruelty, extreme transgression, or extreme deviation from the scriptures.
If one should perform it through delusion, it will immediately go to destruction;
the doer, the one who causes it to be done, the instigator, and the restrainer—
along with their companions, they all shall quickly go to destruction.
For one who performs virtuous deeds, everything such as house and field is not eternal.
For that reason, a mortal should not commit this evil act, even knowing that birth-impurity (sūtaka) will follow once the ritual action has been undertaken. (Ang 1.101)
"One should never omit a constituent part [of the ritual], such is the opinion of Manu, even when an impurity (sūtaka) has occurred for one who has already commenced the rite. (Ang 1.102)
At those respective times, one should perform the ritual limbs; at that moment, one does not become impure due to birth or death. Once that [impurity] has passed, one may proceed again as before.
Even one whose father is living should perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and other ancestral rites such as the Śrāddha; likewise,
he should perform the monthly Śrāddha, the Homa, and the Aṣṭakā rites according to the Pitṛyajña.
After the separation from one's father, one should perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa);
by that, one becomes a performer of the śrāddha rite for the father, not through the offering of cakes for the mother.
If the father is still living when an occasional śrāddha occasion arises,
the son should offer it to those very same ancestors to whom his father would have offered it.
Likewise, while the grandfather is living, he himself should give to those to whom [the grandson] would give;
but his great-grandson should give to those same ancestors in the same manner.
When the father has renounced the world or is defiled by such conditions as loss of caste, the śrāddha is performed for his father and the others.
When his father has renounced the world, fallen, or is of wandering mind and unstable character, the son himself should perform the *śrāddha* rites intended for him. (Ang_1.108)
One who performs the śrāddha rite according to the rules at those respective times does not [suffer];
yet by failing to perform them, he immediately becomes a caṇḍāla. (Ang_1.109)
One who is entitled to perform the *śrāddha* becomes so merely by the offering of the *piṇḍa*;
however, once he has been chosen as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), he would not himself be the performer [of the rite]. (Ang_1.110)
By offering the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) to his father, this person shall become a performer of the śrāddha;
for the sake of establishing his eligibility for the śrāddha, he should perform it on the eleventh day.
Immediately after the father’s attainment of perfection,
the practitioner, having become one with Brahman, should then perform the Pārvaṇa rite for him according to the prescribed rule.
Every year, on the day of accomplishment, one should perform the śrāddha;
thereafter, one should perform the propitiation, or if not on that day, on the following day.
For him who has become Brahman, who possesses the forms of all the gods and so forth,
his status as a father is likewise joined with that very form.
On that day of the śrāddha, one should worship the deity with devotion according to the prescribed rule;
such is the nature of that worship for this rite called śrāddha.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing his eligibility, he should worship him by means of that very [rite].
One should never, under any circumstances, worship one's mother as a father.
Just as the fatherhood residing in the mother—remaining as a single residue—is incapable of performing the function [of a father], so too is that motherhood. Ang_1.117
For the wives of paternal uncles and others possess that very same status as "wife" [relative to their own husbands];
therefore, they are not said to be one's "mothers. (Ang. 1.118)
Even fatherhood and motherhood will come to an end through such giving;
yet, when that [same] action is performed again, they will exist once more as mother and so forth.
For both fatherhood and motherhood reside in one and the same person;
they do not exist elsewhere except through hundreds of thousands of acts.
If one performs an action by invoking the status of "mother" while referring to a secondary mother— motivated by greed for wealth— that [action] will certainly not belong to her. (Ang_1.121)
If, out of greed and delusion, a dull-witted man were to transfer motherhood to other women and perform the ritual acts [toward them], he would immediately become an outcaste (caṇḍāla). Ang_1.122.
If one should intentionally perform a consecration by superimposing reality upon that which is not real,
that ritual act becomes fruitless and he too incurs a fall from his status.
The status of being a father is primary only in relation to one's biological progenitor; in other cases, it is secondary.
If an action is performed by others while placing that [biological relationship] at the forefront, there must be a further ritual act.
Paternity is established solely through the prescribed act of formal acceptance, and not otherwise.
One obtains [the company of] kinsmen with the permission of the king and the learned. // Ang_1.125 //
A brother’s son, having taken a wife and performed the rites,
attains the status of a son through the word of his parents, provided he is free from the distinctions of seniority or juniority [among brothers].
Having taken a wife and performed the rites, he fully acquires the state of a son.
If he alone obtains [the inheritance], the rule for both is not thus;
he would be the primary son of the progenitor, while the other’s son is [only] secondary by virtue of his qualities.
An action should be performed specifically with reference to that person who is primarily related to it by such ties as being a maternal uncle, a paternal uncle, or a son.

If one should perform an action out of negligence, having omitted the primary connection [of the name], one should utter the name of the paternal uncle or others and perform that rite once again. (Ang 1.129)
If one should perform that ritual action while reversing the sequence of the lineage names and the sequence of the temporal succession,
one must indeed perform it again according to the prescribed rule. (Ang 1.130)
If [the recipient] has been initiated, then that action belongs to the initiator by virtue of being the initiator;
it belongs to the giver by virtue of being the one who bestows knowledge; and it belongs to the provider by virtue of being the one who gives the offering. (1.131)
Regarding one who is a source of fear as a source of fear, and regarding one who is a paternal uncle as such [a relative],
having performed the respective utterances for each, one should perform the corresponding ritual action.
If one has performed an act otherwise than it should have been, one should perform it correctly once again. While the primary agent is far away, another may act as a messenger;
however, no one else should act on his behalf in the presence of the principal agent, due to the consequences that would follow for oneself.
Being appointed by him and chosen by him, one should indeed act as his servant;
even if not chosen by him, one may do so as his servant when he has gone abroad.
If the rite has been performed, one should further carry out the ritual intentions and so forth.
Or, if it was performed by another, there is merely the giving of words;
indeed, the son given by word alone, having taken a wife, performs the rites. (1.135)
One should never perform the *darśa* and other such rites for a deceased relative who was a recipient of offerings;
however, one should properly perform only the *śrāddha* rite for his wife and for him.
One should not perform the rites for the deceased ancestors and so forth with great effort every year;
rather, one should diligently perform the rites only for those who are virtuous kinsmen.
One should not perform rites for those who have fallen from their status, the base, the outcaste, or those who neglect their duties; yet one should diligently perform the ritual bath for them.
For those who are non-existent, for the fallen, and for those who have strayed from their caste or are outcaste, impurity is said to end with cremation in ashes;
for those who are degraded or fallen, the authority belongs to the breaking of the water-pot.
[One should avoid] those fallen from their caste, those devoid of ritual action, the fallen, the mother, and the son.

One should abandon a father, a brother, a wife, or even a husband who has become unrighteous toward one another by striking them with a pot; however, one should not act in this manner toward others. This applies specifically to the funeral rites for a deceased person who is without a protector.
By performing the funeral rites for destitute pretas, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha);
here, by the word "saṃskāra," the act of appeasing the pretas is intended.
If one eats out of desire without performing the funeral rites for a deceased person when such rites have not been performed,
one instantly incurs the entire flood of evil karma created by that deceased person. (Ang 1.142)
Then, to pacify those faults, one should perform a ritual bath at the tip of a bow for a full month with diligence; otherwise, one should perform the Ukthya sacrifice.
With the permission of the brahmins, the ascetic should perform his duties; he should especially perform every ritual action with the consent of the brahmins.
This applies to rites for the ancestors and rites for the deceased; otherwise, even for an ascetic, these [rites] do not exist.

Having obtained the permission of the brahmins, the ascetic too, having bathed while still wearing wet clothes, should perform the rites for the deceased; otherwise, that rite is not performed at all.
Even an action performed according to the scriptures that is highly esteemed by many Brahmins,
one should perform it again only with their permission.
If one should perform again that action which was previously defiled by the transgression of hatred and the contempt of many, and which was carried out without his permission.
Furthermore, when an agent is present,
if an action is performed by one who is not the agent— provided that while the agent stands nearby,
that action is carried out for the sake of wealth, livelihood, house, or field— then he would indeed act in such a way. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.148)
There is no impurity for one who has performed the funeral rites for someone not of his own lineage;
yet, he who by any means whatsoever should cremate a deceased person even if they are not of his own lineage,
shall be equal to those of that lineage and remain impure for ten days.
If the anniversary of death for one's mother or father is omitted through delusion, one should perform two *kṛcchra* penances,
as well as ten thousand recitations of the *Gāyatrī* mantra and the *godāna* rite.
Thus, for up to thirty-five years, it is called "mind";
thereafter, O fortunate ones, it falls apart as distinct entities.

Expiation for bathing in a river is prescribed by the virtuous as one hundred baths in a great river when the paternal inheritance has been abandoned; likewise, expiation is said to be through the performance of the purificatory rite (*punaḥsaṃskāra*).
I shall describe to you everywhere, for all purposes, the ritual baths in rivers as a means of expiation for Brahmins who possess Vedic knowledge, with their permission.
For indeed, no atonement has been prescribed that is equal to bathing;
therefore, among all places, bathing at sacred fords and the like is distinguished as superior.
The recitation of the Saṃhitā and so forth, the complete study of the Śruti, or else the chanting of the Vyāhṛtis;
or the chanting of the Gāyatrī, or if not that, the chanting of the Mahārudra. Ang_1.155.
Even the recitation of the *Puruṣasūkta* or the single reading of the *Saṃhitā* has been prescribed by the virtuous as an expiation even for those who have committed grave sins;
such is the majesty of the Veda.
By the utterance of even a single syllable of the Veda, one obtains the fruit of [reciting] all names;
so too for as many names of Hari as are recited by the twice-born.
Even all those countless and infinite waves of impurity would be equal to a single syllable of the Veda, by means of such divine letters.
The Veda, which is essentially Nārāyaṇa himself, is surrounded by immeasurable [beings];
by the recitation of such a Veda, one is freed from all sins.
One who has committed a sin would be liberated immediately; there is no doubt about this.
For such a Veda, the right to study belongs specifically to the Brāhmaṇa. Ang_1.160 //
And there is no authority for anyone else who is merely conditioned by their own actions;
even in that case, it belongs only to one who is completely purified and has performed the daily rites.
Even there, for one who is already purified, on special days as well,
the Veda becomes purer than pure by itself in an instant through its recitation.
The names of the gods are indeed infinite and entirely destructive of evil;
they should be recited repeatedly—of this there is no need for doubt. (Ang 1.163)
Having bathed, one should begin that auspicious Veda;
if one begins it without bathing,
or if out of delusion one should begin it while still unbathed, one becomes a sinner.
Through bathing, all rites are indeed accomplished; of this there is no doubt.
Everything has its root in bathing;
this Vedic bathing is the root of asceticism.
All sacrifices have bathing as their root; this world has bathing as its root.
In all rites and everywhere, bathing alone is considered supreme.

Bathing is proclaimed as the means of purification for all types of impurity; likewise, bathing that constitutes a limb of ritual action is prescribed for touching those who are untouchable, as well as for eating things that should not be eaten.
In this context, [these acts] include the ritualization of the parts (sakalīkaraṇa), as well as defilement (malinīkaraṇa),
making one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa), and other acts that cause loss of caste (jātibhraṃśakara) and so forth.
In all cases of birth-impurity and the like, in all ritual impurities,
and in all penances such as the *kṛcchra* vows, bathing alone is declared to be the supreme remedy.
In all sacrificial sessions (satra) at their beginning and end, that very same [rite] is proclaimed;
likewise, bathing is declared as the remedy for consuming what should not be eaten.
For these individuals who perform improper actions, these primary ablutions shall always be the foremost means of purification.
One should perform this with effort for the sake of purification; otherwise, what purification can there be here?
Upon vomiting, one should bathe;
if it is due to one's own action, one should immediately enter the water with one's clothes on. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.172)
Bathing is prescribed after vomiting due to indigestion when it results from the administration of medicine and other such treatments; however,
there is no bathing required after vomiting unless it has been caused by flies.
One should not engage in bathing; rather, one should diligently perform the washing of that [body] and wear clean garments. Ang_1.174.
In the case of vomiting induced by vegetables, roots, fruits, leaves, pungent, bitter, and other such tastes,
if the vomiting occurs immediately, it will not persist for long. (Ang 1.175)
And when there is vomiting due to illness, then a bath must be performed immediately according to the prescribed rite, following the procedure for the Aghamarṣaṇa.
If vomiting occurs at night— whether due to disease or from indigestion—
a bath in warm water is prescribed before midnight.
"That [sin] shall be expiated only in the morning," so it was said by Śākala;
for in the abandonment of one's own lineage and the adoption of another lineage,
there is both the desertion of one's own gotra and the acceptance of another gotra.
One who has fallen would immediately become pure again through the rite of consecration;
[this involves] the abandonment of one's own lineage and the adoption of a different lineage.
These two have been declared to belong only to women, and not to men:
the Ardhodaya, the Arkavivāha, the Vyatīpāta, and the new moon day occurring during the months of Puṣya and Māgha.
This yoga, which brings about the rise of prosperity, is like ten million suns;
one who has bathed here at Cāpakoṭi would obtain the merit of a hundred baths even if he were to bathe elsewhere.
Having abandoned the duties toward one's father for thirty years, one becomes pure thereafter;
however, if one performs that bath at Mahodaya with devotion a thousand times, [one is purified immediately].
Whether one performs it oneself or causes another to perform it, one becomes pure and freed from prior sin;
otherwise, there is no atonement for such a sinner.
One should carefully examine that practice; therefore, such a woman is indeed a sinner.
If a virtuous wife, through negligence, ascends the funeral pyre with another man, she performs the duty of a son for him who has been cremated by that other. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.184)
"How will that deed be performed by those born in a future age?"—
thus, it is said, the gods remained long absorbed in reflection.
Thereafter, a divine voice arose with clear words and syllables:
"The hardship of union with another man for six years is declared [to be the penance]. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.186)
If she should abandon her life through delusion, the penance for that great sinful deed is declared to be six years,
multiplied by six.
One should always perform this very giving, free from greed and deceit,
specifically for the sake of pacifying the faults associated with the rite known as the "surrender of life.
Having first performed the Cāpāgrayāna, one should perform a hundred ablutions therein.
For a full fortnight, one should practice with diligence, always preceded by what is pleasing.

Its pacification occurs through that [rite] and not by any other means, by means of one thousand five hundred immersions performed with the favor of Brahmins and the recitation of the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* gaṇas.
One should always perform this three times in that very place, and thereafter practice ordinary conduct;
then, through these auspicious deeds, she shall become pure.
Expiation according to the distinction of caste is twofold when associated with a king, threefold through association with a Vaiśya,
and fourfold through association with a Śūdra; thus is expiation declared.
Furthermore, regarding women who have remarried:
if she is remarried by foolish and wicked fathers, brothers, or others, they would all surely go to hell. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.193)
She who has been married twice again is destined for the Mahāraurava hell;
her husband, together with his ancestors, shall go to the Kālasūtra hell.
And the giver incurs the name "one who lies on burning coals.
To atone for that, and to pacify its fault, this supreme expiation is prescribed. (Ang 1.195)
A donor who has gone to Setu, being composed at Dhanuṣkoṭi,
bathing daily at the three sessions of the day and subsisting solely on barley-meal, indeed [attains the goal].
One should dwell for a year with diligent effort, crossing over day by day; speaking of whatever evil one has committed oneself, one should strive thus every single day.
Furthermore, at all sacred fords (tīrtha), he should perform a hundred *taptakṛcchra* penances;
thus he shall become pure, and so too shall the one who carried the corpse.
To pacify that very fault, he should also perform the merit of three *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts.
Exerting effort and remaining vigilant, he should dwell there for three seasons.
Reciting the *gāyatrī* named Drupadā— the mother of the Vedas—
thousands of times during the three junctions of the day, he attained the state of Śiva known as Taptatanu.
Having performed the kṛcchra penance according to the rules and undergone the rite of re-consecration again,
one becomes pure there through the procedure for the womb of the *puṭa*.
If she does not perform the hundred-fold penance, she must undergo re-initiation;
if she abandons two husbands, she must perform a thousand immersions at a sacred bathing place.
And having subsisted on barley-gruel for one year, she is purified;
if she is childless, she becomes possessed of a son, and if she has fallen [from her state], she quickly ascends again with them.
Indeed, she would incur the state of a caṇḍāla through her sons born of that union.
If, due to delusion, a marriage with one's own daughter or the like has occurred, purification comes about solely through one's mother;
likewise, if after a long time and through great hardship caused by delusion or the like, one realizes it was one's own sister or daughter.
If one marries out of delusion, once it is known, one should perform a thousand lunar fasts (cāndrāyaṇa);
thereafter, by means of the bow-tip vehicle, according to the procedure for the interior of the bud.
By performing the rites for birth and other ceremonies for his own mother, he remains pure;
toward others, however, he is equal to a Śūdra, and therefore he may even support her. Having cast aside his former religious duties, he should dwell with her, reciting prayers out of devotion.
If, after a son has been born [to her],
they should procreate through her, one should assign them to the Cāṇḍālas.
Thereafter, he himself should indeed constantly wander the earth subsisting on barley-meal,
confessing his sins and worshipping Hari for as long as he lives.
Dwelling constantly in fields of merit, one should wander through the regions with devotion;
yet, women who have been married or are widows are deceived by great delusion and by deceivers.
If one marries a girl who has been given [in marriage] while knowing that she is [already betrothed], he immediately becomes an outcaste (caṇḍāla);
to pacify that fault, he should perform the same rites as before.
The wise should infer that every duty is doubled;
for she who has been married once, twice, thrice, four times, or five times, [the consequences] are indeed one, two, three, four, or fivefold.
Even if one has correctly understood [the Dharma] during very brief moments or when it is largely obscured by evil, one should nevertheless inquire about it, go forth, and reflect upon it. (1.213)
Having understood its true nature, one should then perform the expiation;
wherever she has gone and with whomever she has been among her own kinsmen.
Having deceived him with illusion and through excessive conduct, she deluded him;
and having recognized each of his [reactions], she conversed with him sufficiently regarding the very root of those words.
Then, after hearing it from the Vedic scholars, she subsequently caused the whole of it to be heard [by others].
Having informed either the king or a kinsman, one should then perform the penance.
In such matters, she would certainly be the field for the first husband alone;
however, she is not at all the supreme [field] for another.
Sometimes, for the sake of religious duties— whether one's own or another's—
a courtesan is superior; yet,
even though she is fit only for pleasure, she is still considered inferior to her [the former].
If, in these matters, one eats in their company at a meal,
or eats together with them, that is considered corrupt and causes one to fall from the state of purity.
For the sake of purifying that [act], one should, according to the Dharma, cover it over in a pit within a river;
having dug either for the duration of a watch (yāma) or for two ghaṭikās.
Therefore, having extracted [the essence] from that, one should subsequently perform the Jātaka and other [narratives],
and according to the Dharma, one should perform thousands of *taptakṛcchra* penances.
One who is self-controlled and subsists on barley-gruel should become pure at the tip of his bow;
he shall perform five thousand ablutions himself or through the mouth of a Brahmin.
One should then practice this for oneself; thus one becomes purely pure, but not others. This is indeed appropriate, as Bhṛgu said of old.
If one who has entered another's body should enter into sexual union, that virtuous woman is purified by consuming barley gruel for three months; not otherwise.
A virtuous woman, having recognized her own husband who has entered into a superior body,
should protect him with special care and must not engage in mere sexual pleasure.
For the connection between two bodies was established long ago in a previous state.
If it is argued that there is no connection between two selves when they reside in different bodies, then [the following applies]:
If one touches a body other than one's own, one does not thereby incur a fall from grace;
for this is true even for the gods, let alone for human beings.
The gods possess both ungraspable forms and graspable forms;
among those with ungraspable and indivisible forms and those with graspable and divisible bodies,
there is a very great difference and a supreme gradation.
It is clearly evident that by this [means], those gods who are ungraspable become manifest;
indeed, the supreme among the supreme gods who possess graspable bodies are to be worshipped.
They are indeed superior and worthy of veneration, and not lowly; therefore,
one should not consider that which is offered as an unacceptable form of worship to be excessively offered to them.
Therefore, a very great offense would not arise;
one should not act in such a way toward those whose forms are ungraspable and indivisible, yet who are presented as graspable and divisible.
For it would always be improper for him, just as the Veda is for a Śūdra;
he should be proficient in the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, or even in those performed for the ancestors.

One should not offer to a deity what has been prepared for another purpose. When there is a mixture of what has been offered and what has not been offered, one should use the offered portion for the sake of enjoyment, but not the unoffered portion. Ang_1.233.
In that same manner, one should again offer salt;
then, having taken it back from the offering, one should [consume it] with ghee.
One should not apply oil or even salt with excessive effort;
one should not make it impure by leaving remnants, nor should one squeeze it with the hand.
One should not break [the rules] through mutual ignorance, nor should one perform that sprinkling;
one should not sprinkle [water] in this manner, but rather silently place it in the mouth.
One should take it from within that [flower], but not even press it with one's teeth;
this is the supreme, pure, and most difficult-to-attain *nirmālya*.
That food, fit even for the gods, should be accepted with great effort and extreme devotion;
at that moment of the great occasion when it has been offered, one should accept the accompanying side-dish as well.
When it comes to consuming the sacrificial oblation (havis) that has been offered for the purpose of partaking in the grace of the Blessed One,
one should not perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (āpośana), nor the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), nor the circumambulatory sprinkling (pariṣecana).
If one should act out of delusion, one will go to the Raurava hell;
having removed cooked food from the main dish and placed it in a separate vessel, [one should offer it]. (Ang 1.240)
Having made it pleasantly warm and prepared it, one should subsequently offer it with branches and other ingredients; however,
if it is offered while excessively hot,
it is either unbearably hot, extremely hot, or has merely reached the cooking vessel.
He who, out of delusion, offers food to a deity shall become a denizen of hell; therefore, one should remove the food intended for offering and place it separately in another vessel. Ang_1.242.
Having made it pleasantly warm with effort, having formed it into a mound, and having sprinkled it with clarified butter—
[the rice] which is exceedingly pure, most excellent, fit for a king, and most beautiful.
One should offer to the deity food accompanied by vegetables, side dishes, and fruits;
thereafter, with a concentrated mind, one should also carefully give that same food [to others].
Without sprinkling water or performing the ritual lustration, and likewise without offering the oblation of breath, one who is himself pure should carefully offer even the remnants of food.
The manner of acceptance:
one should not chew the offered substances with the teeth, nor break them, nor make a sound; rather, one should consume them silently, like water. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.246)

One should eat fruits that are flavorful with effort, and one should not make a sound; even when eating fruits that are as hard as wood, one should do so with care and without making a noise from the throat.
One should give to children, indeed one should give to children; if one does not accept it oneself, that is well.
But if one should accept it, then one should sit at night in a pure place.
Without making a sound, he indeed gratified her with news and other such matters;
for one staying in a cave, bathing at night with warm water is forbidden,
as a householder should not bathe at night, or if he does bathe, it must be with water.
In the hot season, when permitted by a Brahmin and witnessed by the fire, one who is able should not bathe with hot water; however, if he is unable, he may do so. Ang_1.250.
One who has been anointed with oil should likewise bathe for the sake of bodily health;
that is called "anointing-bath" by the virtuous, and therefore one should not perform it daily.

Therefore, there is no performance of occasional rites (*naimittika*) even for the gods until the flood of daily and other obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) has been completed according to the prescribed rule.
Afterwards, there is the anointing and bathing; however, if that is not possible at the midday time, one should perform such a bath at midday or during the *saṃgava* period.
Having performed the midday bath— the ritual re-bathing for the midday observance according to the rules—
one should then commence that rite; therefore, one should not perform this [midday] rite [again].
For that bathing is proclaimed as being for the purpose of removing impurities;
likewise, the razor-bath is said to be unsuitable for ritual action.
If one performs a Vedic rite after shaving and bathing, but without another subsequent bath, one shall not obtain the fruit thereof. (Ang 1.256)
One might even incur a transgression by doing so; therefore, a wise person should not act in this way.
One should not perform an oil massage or a bath in the morning, evening, or on festival days;
one should not apply oil in the morning, evening, or on festival days.
During eclipses, at times of ancestral rites (śrāddha), during all religious observances (vrata),
during meritorious Vedic initiations, and in sacred fields or holy fords, one should not eat at night.
Having slept, eaten, or wept; having traveled a long distance; being thirsty, excessively hungry, or afflicted by illness—one should under no circumstances perform [the recitation]. (Ang 1.259)

Having failed to perform his daily duties, having been made to vomit [his food], having been severely beaten, having been cursed after cursing [others], and having caused other men to be killed under a pretext; // Ang_1.260 //
One should never take the wealth of the destitute;
nor, having sent away one's own kin and humiliated one's teachers and relatives, should one ever act [in such a way].
When those duties that must necessarily be performed according to the scriptures have indeed presented themselves as great obligations, yet one fails to perform them out of sheer folly— Ang_1.262.
A twice-born man should never hastily perform the rubbing of the body with unguents;
rather, he should first perform the *nāndī-śrāddha* accompanied by a water-pot, and only after that, following the *sodaka-kumbha-śrāddha*, should he proceed with the anointing and bathing.

one who has already bathed should not perform the *snāna* again, nor ever the *śrāddha*s.
One should not perform the *nāndī* with those two; that is remembered as being done only by way of an alternative rule (*anukalpa*).
For one who is incapable, bathing with ointment may at times serve as a substitute for bathing.

It is said that for the performer of the *nāndī-śrāddha* accompanied by the water-pot, the merit of bathing in a river located one *krośa* away is attained; however, one should not perform a *śrāddha* for one's parents [if such a river is available], because of the rule regarding bathing in a river situated at a distance of one *krośa*.

Furthermore, after the great purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) following the *śāva* (impurity of death) and the immersion during the rainy season, one should immediately perform that rite known as the *śrāddha* by bathing at his [the deceased's] body. (Ang. 1.267)

In every case, for any ritual action, one should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), which consists of the verbal utterance "I shall do this," preceded by the regulation of the breath (prāṇāyāma) according to the mantra. Ang_1.268.

One should not perform any action—whether obligatory, optional, or otherwise—without a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*). That resolve should first be mental, and subsequently it should be expressed verbally.
By the sentence beginning with "yasya" (of whom), the auspicious Śruti has likewise stated that both place and time must be mentioned there, provided they are relevant to the resolve.
The lunar day (tithi) is declared to be time; if that [time] is transposed, the ritual act is immediately destroyed. Therefore, one must perform it again. Ang_1.271 //
If there is a reversal in the order of the ancestral rites for the fathers, one should perform them again;
when the śrāddha for both parents falls on the same day,

If one performs a *śrāddha* out of delusion on a day that is not the proper day, one should perform it again; likewise, if it was performed on an empty lunar day (*śūnyatithi*), one should perform it again with effort on an empty lunar day. Ang_1.273 //
This defect of an empty lunar day at the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka) never occurs for the performance of a śrāddha rite; therefore, one should perform it precisely then.

On a single day, even if a man is beset by hardship, he should always perform the *śrāddha* for his mother and father with food on their anniversary of death;
he should never do so using only [water] and the like. (Anga 1.277)

This practice of eating at that time would not be a fault for anyone among all the castes or those dwelling in any of the stages of life.

By all those [criteria], they are to be understood as entirely distinct types of men according to the intended classification:

Prajāpati has declared that the abandonment of food leads to such a fault.

Therefore, one should not be patient [with such a person]; rather, one should act against him beforehand.

One who has a son is considered to possess the sacred fire; one who has a son is eternally possessed of the fire; one who has a son is remembered as a true possessor of Vedic learning (śrotriya).
A daughter who is a direct knower of Brahman makes one truly possessed of a son and fortunate;
for whatever virtues exist in oneself, they all reside in this son from that very moment.
They will have been accomplished; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
He is not one who possesses a son but lacks a wife; rather, he is this very man who lacks a son.
One who possesses no fire is not a true son, and one who has no son is considered to possess no fire.
Through a son, the gift of immovable property and the gift that bears fruit become truly fruitful.
Whatever great thing in the world is difficult for all to obtain, one who possesses a son may attain it;
therefore, one should always perform the auspicious rites for the sake of a son, both Vedic and worldly. Ang_1.321.

Therefore, one who is healthy should never neglect his wife when she is in her season; if that fool neglects her, he incurs the sin of foeticide. On the day she has bathed after her period, whether he be a youth or a learned Vedic scholar, he should approach her.
It would not even be fit for poetry if it were actually to happen that one possesses a son.
Beholding the face of the newborn son:
by the mere birth of a son, this man becomes released from his debt;
therefore, upon the birth of a son, a man should immediately look upon his face. (Ang_1.324)
For one who does not see it, liberation from debt does not arise through mere talk;
therefore, a person should act by whatever means possible.
If he is weak, especially so, the wise man should effect the procreation of a son;
or he may designate as his own one given for service, or even one given at the time of the investiture with the sacred girdle.

If it is not otherwise, one who has been given [as a son] at a marriage or at a sacrifice saves eight lineages; one given for the sake of livelihood saves sixteen, and one given at the investiture of the sacred girdle saves thirty-two.
Yajñadatta, who was given [the bride] in marriage, will cross over thirty-two [families];
indeed, by his mere effortless play, he shall immediately deliver sixty-four families.
He who, by means of the livelihood granted by one who has no son, fully maintains his life-sustenance, is known as Vṛttidatta; such a son secures for him the worlds of merit.
Indeed, whatever wealth might be brought to him in this world,
his son named Mauñjidatta was even more excellent than that.
In the same way, there may be another son who secures the next world;
he is known as the "son given at marriage" (*vivāhadatta*), and the one beyond him is twice as superior.
Beyond that was his son Yajñadatta, who was dear to his father;
all these sons exist solely for the fulfillment of their respective duties,
which they accomplish through the giving of wealth, and not otherwise.
Therefore, it is said that the virtuous consider wealth to be the sole result of these actions.
Great-souled ones who desire to see the next world do not accept [wealth] by gathering it bit by bit from various sources through righteous people.
And over a long period of time, one should perform them gradually;
for when these great deeds have been performed in this manner, [the goal is attained].
One should not have many sons; therefore, one should act accordingly toward them.
Regarding others, the term "son" applies only when a son is difficult to obtain among those of the same lineage (sagotra) or the same ancestry (sapiṇḍa). Ang_1.336.
One may take up what has been heard among kinsmen, others, or those of different castes;
however, one should perform the grasping among those of the same caste, and not take it up from those of a different caste. Ang_1.337
By performing this with those of a different caste, one falls from one's own caste immediately;
if one adopts a son of a different *gotra*,
that adopted son represents three generations of his own lineage.
Immediately thereafter, that family attains its purpose;
otherwise, it falls into confusion, yet if one exerts effort, it will cross over.

One who does not belong to the same lineage (asagotra) should not be accepted as an heir, for he would become the very owner of the recipient; the inheritance goes to him, while the progeny belongs only to the giver.

Therefore, after the birth of his own sons, he should cause those sons given away (datta) to enter the lineage of their biological father alone at the tying of the girdle (mauñjī), by means of the sacred mantras. If he does not cause the sons given away to enter his own lineage, [he incurs a fault].
Or those born of a given [father], or those born of him, or those born of both of his lineages—let them be yours.
In marriage, there is the relinquishing of both lineages; this being so, when birth has occurred here and the pressing of hands (marriage) has arrived,
one should then properly and with effort relinquish both lineages.
Indeed, for the sake of knowing the lineage, the two types of marriage, and the meaning of the dharma, one should perform that pair of Ārṣa marriages for those born of such [lineages]. Ang_1.344.
In the case of salutation and similar acts, there is a dual lineage (dvigotra) in constant salutation, twilight worship (saṃdhyā-vandana), and optional salutation; however,
in the case of the complete ancestral lineage (ārṣeya), there is a single lineage even when the other belongs to a different lineage.
Having accepted two ancestral lineages (ārṣa) and joined them together, one should thereafter state only a single lineage; likewise, one may state one, two, or three ancestral lineages.
This [field] shall be five or seven *arṣakas*, or nine or eleven *arṣakas*;
thus there shall be one *gotra* consisting of thirteen *arṣakas*.
In this way, the fifteen lineages (gotra) were produced from that;
indeed, the lineages thus born arose from the provision of sustenance.
Therefore, having investigated and questioned those who belong to the same lineage on this earth, one should abandon that doubt, for there are only this many [lineages] upon the earth.
There are indeed lineages established by the scriptures that have one ṛṣi, some that have two ṛṣis, those with three ṛṣis, and even those with five ṛṣis. Ang_1.350 //
Only these many [means] are established everywhere by the scriptures, and nothing else;
they exist solely through the lineage transmitted from the original bestower to those who received them.
Brāhmaṇas are seen to have a lineage extending back seventeen generations;
therefore, since the former gotra belongs to those such as the *dattaja* (given son), one should cause the *dattaja* sons to enter into that former gotra.
If, even without entry [into the womb], they were to attain the supreme state as members of the same lineage,
then— due to delusion— that would have occurred previously for both the father and the son.
Since this is so, one must avoid [marrying into] a lineage at the time of marriage and other such occasions;
for if one does not know the prior history of that lineage and its progenitor, [one should refrain]. (Ang_1.354)
If one were to marry her, it would surely result only in great misfortune;
therefore, once the past history is known, one should abandon her and treat her as one would a mother.

One should indeed protect [the kingdom] according to the Dharma, and afterwards perform the threefold penance (kṛcchra) to eliminate that fault; however, if those [beings] were born there [in hell], then [one must act accordingly].
The conclusion is that one should resolutely apply oneself only to the Caṇḍālas;
therefore, one should by no means accept a son who is not of the same lineage (asagotra).
But a wise man who knows the Dharma and understands the distinctions between preceding and succeeding rules should,
according to the scriptures, perform the adoption of a son only among those of his own lineage (*sagotra*);
however, marriage, fire-offerings (*homa*), and other such rites are not permitted with respect to the sons of one's brothers.
Among the offspring of one’s brother, there should be no marriage, nor acceptance [of them as sons], nor hospitable treatment;
nor indeed should rites such as the *homa* be performed for them. Their status as sons exists only by word alone.
Regarding the possession of brothers, sons, and so forth:
while one's brothers and sons are present, one should not likewise accept other kinsmen;
nor should one accept those who have gone far away, for such a person is indeed a thief.
At the time of taking up a son, however, one should satisfy the minds of his parents with gifts and other means for the sake of what is to be done in the future.
And having made a firm oath with his kinsmen, the king, and other people,
he further established this boundary for his son as well.
Even if a biological son has already been born, I shall certainly do this again without a doubt;
having first made it firm myself, I shall thereafter adopt that son as my own.
If he does not do so, there will undoubtedly be a very great fault:
"Immediately after having adopted [another's son], if a biological son is born; or if, after having adopted another's son, a biological son is subsequently born. (Ang_1.364)

Having acted otherwise than what was previously stated out of delusion, and now practicing that which is harmful while uttering those wicked words against me—may this man truly not exist today. (Ang_1.365)
If a wicked and extremely cruel person should speak thus, by which the earth becomes excessively burdened,
a righteous king should strike him and banish him from the country;
he should confiscate his entire property if it does not belong to that local community.
It is said that the rain-god Parjanya will not send rain, and even turmoil within the kingdom arises.
Whatever was said at the time of the gift of the son must be carried out;
that speech which was uttered by the parents' recipient at the time of the gift of the son cannot be disregarded later.
By his kinsmen, by that king, by those people who give or cause others to give, by his wives, by his sons, or indeed by anyone else; (1.369)
Furthermore, at the time of granting a son, one must not transgress the words spoken thereafter, whether they concern a small or great matter, or what is possible or impossible. Ang_1.370 //
That which is foolish is for one who, having previously declared firmly before people for his own sake, now strives to make it otherwise. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.371)
Having incurred the sin of killing an embryo, they indeed did not go to the higher world;
desiring the welfare of their own sons, they disregarded the command of their husband or father, which had been previously proclaimed by their husband.
Those who suddenly disregard the words previously spoken by their husband or father will indeed be partakers of hell. (Ang_1.373)
Whether it be his wife or his son, out of folly he may utter falsehood prompted by folly—something ill-heard, harsh, cruel, and contrary to our purpose. (Ang_1.374)
Nor did we accept the words of that wicked speaker; having rebuked him with our speech, censured him, and struck him on both cheeks, we dismissed him. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.375)
One should quickly banish [such a person] from the country and properly honor the virtuous.
Regarding the acceptance of a brother or a son, one who has been accepted as a brother’s son and the biological son born later shall have equal shares.
It is always declared that [the inheritance] for one who is not a kinsman is an equal share; however, if it is for another who is a kinsman (sagotra), it is a fourth part.
Thus did Pitāmaha declare that for a kinsman and others, it is a fourth part.
The biological son, though younger in age, is indeed the elder; of this there is no doubt.
But when the protector-father has passed away, one who is adopted is superior in age.
Whether he has brought a wife, or has fathered a son, or is performing a sacrifice—
if he does not with effort cause that [son] to be initiated, then the one given (datta) is considered his legitimate son (aurasa).
For although this one is younger by age, he has been given [the status of] the youngest according to the Dharma;
yet even though he is inferior in age, the biological son is the eldest—of this there is no doubt.
When a son given in adoption (dattaka) has been initiated, he is thereafter called "given" (datta); but one born later according to the law is the elder brother.
If, out of delusion, one who is deficient in the sacred law should initiate such a person as the elder, he does not perform the rite properly.
For through negligence they might indeed bring them together, and both would certainly fall;
yet there can never be any mutual union between the two.
The taking of a son by one whose wife has died, by an ascetic, or by a student:

a woman whose husband has died, a female ascetic, a trusting woman, or one whose husband is far away—none of these should adopt a son; likewise, even a woman whose husband is far away should not do so while she is in a state of birth-impurity (sūtakī).
The authority belongs to both husband and wife together;
it never exists separately in the giving or the receiving of that [gift].
If there were a union of two pairs of entities occupying the positions of the birth canal and the organ of procreation,
that would constitute the giving and receiving of a son.
If the mind is unshakable, steady, and contented— finding its pleasure in the pair of the womb and the place of birth— then indeed one should practice that very state.
The couple, having satisfied the other's mind with garments and other gifts,
made a firm oath for the sake of their future undertaking.
Having formally declared it before witnesses, in the presence of deities and brahmins,
and having informed the king and their kinsmen, they should then take the son.
Having made a promise at that time, if one fails to fulfill it,
then after the oath has been sworn, let men not transgress the boundaries previously established for the duration;
the king shall banish them from the kingdom.
Among wives, she who is present at the time of the son's adoption is his mother; any other co-wife who stands at a distance during the adoption becomes his "Ambā" (stepmother).
The mother with a co-wife remains at a distance; it is not otherwise.
If other relatives, such as her mother or maternal grandfather,
should be present— whether two or three— then she should,
with a devoted heart, perform it together with her husband for the sole purpose of pleasing him, who takes delight in having sons.
All mothers are to be known as his; he indeed has many mothers, having at that time adopted [all beings] as his children—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (Ang 1.392)
And all their fathers are considered his maternal grandfathers;
therefore, in all śrāddha rites, one should [offer] to all the maternal grandfathers in due order.
One should join them within that very same funeral cake, or separately;
or one may cast the cakes for those ancestors who are merely remembered here. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.394)
Since all verbal expressions are equal, conceptual construction is indeed the same;
one may perform it according to one's preference, or just as it was previously established.
In the same way, one should act subsequently; for this is the settled rule everywhere:
the father of a co-wife is not a maternal grandfather, and the father of a co-wife’s mother likewise would not be a maternal grandfather.
Regarding the libation for the mother of a co-wife:
the mother of a co-wife receives two handfuls (añjali) during the daily libation; she [the wife] shall never receive even a single handful as she would her own mother. [050] Ang_1.397
The wife of one who has remarried shall receive two handfuls;
whether she is childless or has children, she is declared to be equal to that [share]. (Ang_1.398)
One should perform the Śrāddha for her in the *aupāsana* fire; one should perform the Śrāddha in the *aupāsana* fire, not in a common (*laukika*) fire.
If one should perform it through negligence, his lineage will perish. (Ang 1.399)
Since the day a wife dies has been declared to be equal to the day her father perishes, who indeed would be so deluded as to [neglect] her? (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.400)
A wise man should perform [the rite] in the worldly fire according to his own tradition;
that [tradition] is indeed his wife while she is alive, but if she has died, it belongs to the class of his mother.
Regarding the procedure for taking a brother’s son as a son:
having seen his wife after a long time since their marriage was performed,
he should wait twelve years from the first appearance of her menses before obtaining this [son].
This is declared to be the primary seizure by the spirit Putra; this is the procedure for that seizure.
The virtuous have declared that the *pravara* (lineage) is interrupted if there is a break in it;

consequently, the son would become inferior by two or three degrees of such division. Thus, a brother’s son becomes inferior because he does not immediately receive the nourishment of the mother’s milk.
But because he grasps that [mind] as "I," a son is born who is inferior to him.
In this way, for the other nine [initiations], after the *jātahoma*, that which is less than that is given separately according to the difference of days; thus, O son, he becomes a *putraka*.
Therefore, if the eldest has a son who is inferior to him, there is no doubt in this matter;
nor [is he the heir] if a brother is separated by one, two, or three divisions.
His son shall likewise be deficient in the same way;
furthermore, the sons of a stepmother are to be ranked according to seniority.
Those sons are indeed deficient according to the path of the scriptures;
likewise, the various kinds of nephews and their sons are also deficient.

Those who are fewer than that are likewise said to be of the same lineage (sagotra). Indeed, they should be understood as such; however, what if they belong to different lineages (bhinnagotra)? Furthermore: [Ang_1.410]
What more need be said? Having understood this, a wise person, after carefully considering the time and place, should undertake the care of his son according to the prescribed rule.
Upon division, the brothers are equal; for their sons are indeed equal to them. Having received [their shares], they do not obtain a fourth part when a son is born.
They receive an equal share, for they are equal to the legitimate son;
the wise declare that a legitimate son is one born of a lawful wife.

One born from a second wife and so forth cannot attain equality with him; those who discourse on Brahman declare that the son born of a wedded wife is the legitimate (aurasa) son of one begotten through desire.
They say that all sons born of other wives, beginning with the second, are born of desire;
however, the son of the lawful wife attains seniority and shall receive respect due to one who has been given [in marriage].
Even one born later who is younger in age, if he is a second or subsequent son,
becomes equal to the sons of the lawful wife in regard to ancestral rites and the like after a certain period of time.
Although they exist, there is no doubt; nevertheless, I shall further declare that which is singular: from that [cause] having arisen, it becomes the performer of its own effect.
A son given away by his father, even if he is advanced in age, shall have no authority over the father's affairs,
whether the father is still living or not, provided that there exists a lawful wife.
If the performer of the rite has two wives, [the rite may be performed] for one of them;
or if a son has been given by one of the two, [it may be performed] for that one who is the performer of the rite.
Manu has indeed declared that this [son] would be equal to a legitimate son of the body (aurasa) if he were a daughter's son who has been given away, or likewise one born of a brother. (AngL 1.420)
Constantly weighed against his own body, those two who were ever devoted to the Dharma were declared to be the perpetual recipients of what was given by Datta, as if they were his very parents.
Even the status of being a father does not remain with one's biological parents once [the child] has been given away;
therefore, after the act of giving and the fire-offering, those two are considered his true parents.
For both fatherhood and motherhood reside in one and the same person;
they do not exist elsewhere except through hundreds of thousands of such acts.
When fatherhood has passed to the mother, the single remainder is diminished;
just as that [remainder] is incapable of performing the function of a father, so too is the motherhood [incapable].
Indeed, the same would apply to the wifehood of a paternal uncle’s wife and others.
Therefore, that [state] does not belong to them; hence, one should not speak of that as motherhood.

For among the Prajāpatis, one who is the son of a paternal uncle or the son of a paternal grandfather, or even one of the same lineage (*sagotra*), may be either elder or younger; yet he cannot be both one and many, nor can he belong to a different lineage or be a hater of his own lineage.
Any son who has come from a man of the same lineage and is accepted as such, and who is devoted to his mother’s womb, shall be considered a son; he would not be a son born of pride.

A student (varṇin) has a wife who is his lawful spouse and sons; a householder has sons from a second wife and so forth; and even one who has fathered a son and established the sacred fires is not equal to the student in every respect.

A young son of a lawful wife, a youth who is the son of a second wife and so forth, one who has maintained the sacred fires, and one with ten sons—none of these were urged by the whole [assembly]. Ang_1.429.
He alone is the primary performer of the ancestral rites (pitrkṛtya), there is no doubt;
even if he has not yet been initiated (anupeta), everything [is accomplished] through his performance of those rites.
If that supreme rite is to be performed, it should be done with the eldest son at the head;
for as soon as a son by the lawful wife is born, all other sons are considered secondary.
Indeed, those born in the second and subsequent cities would arise at that very moment,
both through the birth of a lawful wife and son, and by the performance of their assigned duties.
For the second and subsequent sons, immediate loss of caste (*hainya*) would occur as declared by the Vedas,
provided that he performs the ritual duties for the wife of the second son;
however, there is a distinction in the case of those given away (*datta*) and so forth.

If the adopted son is superior [in merit], or even more so than his father—whether the biological father is absent or present while still living—the adopted son [is the one to offer the funeral cake]. (Ang 1.434)
If he performs the duties of her husband, he is considered the husband of her daughter;
but if he is the son of a second wife, then he is the adopted son who performs the duties.
If he is not the eldest son, he immediately incurs disgrace;
for the father and his lawful wife are always equal to the one who has been given away.
If there is no son, his other wives are to be consecrated;
but when a son exists, he alone shall perform that rite, and not another.
It has always been declared thus; for this reason, he is not weak, since the ritual was performed by him for his first wife after she had been given away.
If, according to the son of Satyanyāya, this [result] were greater by that much alone, then even a fourth part would be equal; such is the karma performed by him.
Therefore, when a son has been given [in adoption], the wise man born of the youngest wife should himself perform the rites for the eldest wife’s husband.

When a rite has been performed for that field or for the father by the eldest son or an adopted son, the merit thereof belongs to him, and it is greater than that of his [the father's] other sons. (Ang_1.441)
If the father is present, and if this elder brother of his is also present before him,
then the merit of the deed is indeed accomplished by the gift, and he would immediately become superior even to a son.
If the father’s duty has been performed by means of what was given while sons exist,
then he does not acquire any superior ownership over it.
