This is so even if that gift was made to his eldest wife who is without a son.
Surely that karma must have been bestowed upon him in excess of what was due from his son.
If that supreme deed was performed by the father through what was given by him,
then even though he is the primary agent, the son alone would not be the primary one.
Among all sons, this one born of the wife of the body (aurasa) indeed excels;
regarding the specific types of wives,
among them is the lawful wife (dharmapatnī).
The legitimate son is one born of the lawful wife, and the lawful wife is she who is exclusively [so].
Whomever he previously married— whether she was ignorant or possessed of bad qualities—
that alone is declared by those who know the Dharma to be his lawful wife.
A second wife who follows after her— whether she be of noble birth, beautiful, or advanced in age—
is not his lawful wife; she is declared to be a concubine.
If there is a son and a bed, yet she is married again out of desire, that second woman who enjoys the pleasures is not considered a lawful wife. (Ang_1.449)
Regarding the seniority and juniority among sons,
it is recorded in the Smṛti that the son born of the lawful wife is the eldest;
she alone is the one who effects the marriage for him who otherwise lacks a wife or offspring.
She who, though married, has been urged toward a religious marriage for the sake of dharma while there exists a husband,
or a son, grandson, great-grandson, or even a lineal descendant; (1.451)
When she is established, she who is called Ūḍhā is the consort of Bhogin, named Kāñcanā;
and all the names of Bharmaṇa, including Āvātā and others, belong entirely to her. (Ang. 1.452)
Therefore, she is called the second [type], named Kāñcanā;
she does not become a lawful wife, but is remembered as merely a concubine.
Since she is to be won over through persuasion, she is therefore remembered as *vanitā*;
and because she is to be addressed with all manner of golden words, she is proclaimed as *vāvātā*.
One obtains all those evil reputations that are notorious on the earth; they know that third [rebirth] as such.
Some declare that "transformation" (parivṛtti) is to be understood as "the stainless one" (vimalā); the exponents of Brahman call it the yellow, the tawny, and the auspicious one.
All their sons were progressively weaker;
being inferior to the sons of their lawful wives, they were even more deficient in age.
She was the first lawful wife, fortunate and the chief queen; indeed, she was described by those who know the Dharma as Satkarṇī and Kalyāṇī. (Ang_1.458)
Even a young son of a lawful wife, though he may not yet have been invested with the girdle of muñja grass,
[is entitled to the inheritance] even while other sons remain, even if those others have been honored by their own ritual acts.
He is the most excellent in rites for the ancestors; therefore, he is the one who bestows the sacred fire.
Whatever principal rite there may be, it is all performed through his agency.
O sons, it is right that you all should cause all the mantras to be performed correctly according to the prescribed ritual;
for in this way, the entire great Dharma is fulfilled.
However, what has been ordained by him in brief has not yet been fully accomplished.
In that case, my dear, the deceased father does not find the world beyond.
Yet, not being liberated from the state of a preta, he is exceedingly tormented by hunger and thirst;
wandering, running, stumbling, and roaming, he seeks refuge anywhere at all. Ang_1.463.
In the world of the departed (preta), he is indeed constantly turned face-downward, longing for water;
afflicted by disease, shaven-headed, deformed, dull-witted, wandering, and dejected in mind.
Therefore, he alone truly dwells perpetually [within him], for he is the very son of his own breast; whereas one born of a lawful wife possesses only the capacity for physical contact,
being produced by a lawful wife yet whose caste remains unknown.
Upon merely touching the funeral rites for a deceased person, one should bathe and perform them without mantras;
by that alone, my dear, one has fulfilled his duty and becomes exceedingly happy.
He attains true fatherhood and becomes eternally blissful;
those very sons of their respective mothers are declared to be the primary agents.
Since biological sons possess primacy, they alone are declared to be supreme;
they are the performers of those respective rites, and not those born of other mothers.
When the lawful wife and young son are present—though perhaps lacking letters, with indistinct or distinct syllables—or indeed when they have passed away; ||| Ang_1.469 ||
By a son belonging to the next generation,
or by anyone who is his equal, or by a brother, a disciple, or another relative.
Whatever principal rite there may be in this or that context, all of it should be performed for this child with the mantra;
its presence consists merely in being the agent through touch.
Only a mere touch should be performed, and merely its presence alone is required here for the sake of providing the sole cause of great satisfaction to the deceased. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.472)
Merely by the touch of its proximity, he who has died shall indeed partake in happiness; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, one should practice that very thing. (Ang_1.473)
These have been declared by the great-souled ones as the "savers" (tāraka) for one who has died;
indeed, these are remembered as the causes of great satisfaction.

The five syllables beginning with *ja* provide extreme satisfaction at the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and other ceremonies; furthermore, there is the presence of the offspring of the lawful wife, as well as the performance of her duties and the ancestral rite of reception (*grahaṇa-śrāddha*). Ang_1.475.
The *śrāddha* at Gayā under the asterism Phalgunī, as well as the *śrāddha* with vegetables,
likewise the propitiation of Gaurī, and the ritual release of a bull.
The Mahālaya and the Panasa—these are all supreme;
they have declared them to be the sole causes for ultimate satisfaction and liberation. (Ang_1.477)
In that regard, there is a pentad beginning with the birthplace for the letter *ta*;
this first [pentad] is the savior for the deceased, while the subsequent one is indeed for the legitimate son.
At the time of death, however, there may be the presence of a second or subsequent son, or whatever else may be conducive to the deceased's welfare in the next world. (Ang_1.479)
In this way, the ritual action for the deceased, preceded by mantras, becomes effective;
likewise, there may be the *grahaṇa-śrāddha* and the other, the *gayā-śrāddha*.
The *phālgunī-śrāddha* performed with one hundred and eight [offerings] grants satisfaction;
furthermore, the *śrāddha* performed with vegetables is singularly efficacious for crossing over [to liberation].
The gift of Gaurī brings satisfaction to the ancestors;
the gift of Gaurī is the release of a bull; this Mahālaya rite occurs every fortnight; and the installation of the one named Panasa—these indeed are remembered as such. (Anga 1.482)
"O child, they say that the five *ja*-sounds are indeed dear even to all the ancestors for one who has gone to the other world. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.483)
For the sake of satisfaction and for crossing over, he spoke thus and nothing else:
the five *ja*s, half of *jala*, the bank of the Jāhnavī, and the great remembrance of Janārdana. (Ang 1.484)
The blazing one, birth, arising, son, and proximity—these five syllables beginning with *ja* are proclaimed; they are said to be the liberators from birth.
Regarding the characteristics of the śrāddha performed during an eclipse:
when one, surrounded by his wife and others, performs such a śrāddha with food immediately upon touching the eclipse for the satisfaction of the ancestors; [that is the grahaṇa-śrāddha].
Having bathed according to that very same procedure, the Śrāddha for the planets is said to be performed;
indeed, this was taught by the Lord of Gods, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings.
The Lord of All declared that even a hundred great gifts do not equal sixteen śrāddhas performed by the high-souled Gaya.
The śrāddha at Gayā, at Phalgunī, and with kāśa herbs are indeed equal to these;
likewise is the gift of a Gaurī and the ritual release of a bull. Ang_1.489
"Great and inactive," so say Manu, Kātyāyana, Aṅgiras, Kutsa, Vatsa, Agni, Bharata, Viśvāmitra, Śuka, and others. (Ang. 1.490)
There exists no other paternal duty equal to these, even in the three worlds; therefore, one should practice each of them with supreme devotion.
"May he too be a doer who has accomplished his purpose, a man of merit, and a savior of his ancestors"—
thus did they rejoice at him who had established the breadfruit tree.
We do not know who he was— whether he was Dūrvāsas,
Janaka, or Dadhīci born from a jar, or Śibi, Nahuṣa, or Nala.
Whether it be Māndhātṛ, or Alarka, or the great Hariścandra,
or Gaya, or the illustrious Rāma— if not even one among these.
There is no doubt that Brahmā, Śiva, and Hari have descended here upon the surface of this earth as the collective totality of these [deities] for the welfare of the worlds.
When the jackfruit was placed [on the scale], there was a great difference; those standing behind that unripe fruit spoke to the one who had placed it there:
"All [the thorns] have been constantly clinging to it in the form of thorns. (Ang 1.496)
Because one hundred and eight specific divine vegetables for the śrāddha rites proceed from it, at that time there is a "thousandfold vegetable" (śākasahasraka).
Of this one of divine form, whose very life is his father’s breath,
who embodies all the gods, who consists of all mantras,
and whose radiant body is the essence of all sacrifices, great holy sites, rivers, and fires;
Of those who subsist on the nectar of the penances prescribed by the flood of all the scriptures and treatises.
The installation of the purifying treasure, which has the form of a paternal magnet,
is performed by means of the roots of the *chāyāpatra* tree.
Satisfaction for the ancestors may be brought about by means of fruits, or even by unripe shoots, wood, or even shadows; this occurs whether done intentionally or unintentionally. (Ang 1.501)
Even by the venerable Brahmā or by the King of Serpents, it would not be possible to describe the fruit of his merit even in a thousand years.
It is said that in ancient times, all the *śāka* trees, desiring to satisfy their ancestors,
performed austerities and then, by means of a boon from Brahmā, took refuge in the *panasa* tree.
Alarka-śrāddha, Alaka, Alarka, Kārūṣa, Acyuta, Cūta, Anara, and Amara—
among these seven, if Acyuta is present, then Alarka and the three Ajas are also present.
The twelve classes are remembered according to their monthly divisions;
therefore, the number for these three is thirty-six.
Among these month-born [fruits], there may be those that are single-seeded and unripe;
and by the division of those eleven types of unripe fruits,
a twofold classification is indeed repeatedly established for the unripe fruit as well.
It has come to possess a twofold nature through the distinction between the moist and the dry.
Likewise, fruits are further divided into two types;
among them, the citron and the myrobalan are to be taken until autumn, along with the purifying [substances].
Divine vegetables fit for ancestral rites include vāruka, karmaja, śāri, śrīparṇa, śrīkara, śamī, yugada,
yugmada, ramya, vajraparṇī, and karīṣakī.
Kāravallī, Trayī, Kāru, Kāmakṛt, Kāmavāraka, Kāmavāhī, Kāmadūra, and Śākuṭa—these two are the foremost. (Ang_1.510)
Kāmapra, Kāmada, Kamra, Kaliṅga, Kalivāruka,
Ajaśrī, Ajacarma, Dāruka, Dharmada, and Dama.
Manu is the maker of the lineage, Nala is the crest-jewel of royal splendor;
he is the one who fashions the stalk, the one to be consumed, the singer of the Gāyatrī, and the one with tawny eyes.
He who has bay horses, whose neck is like a horse, who is compassion, who loves gold,
who holds the bow, who performs actions, who is the object of action, who bestows fortitude, who creates honor, and who is the maimed one.
Śaracchrīka, Maṅgalaka, Kuṇḍa, Akuṇḍa, Guḍapriya, Phalaśrī, Madhuragrīva, Dānada, Kaṭuka, Kṣamī,
Mānmatha, Madhurasrāvā, Vajraghna, and Vajrapañjara.
Born from an anthill, Bālarāja, Bālaputra, and Bṛhadratha.
Karṇakāra destroys eye diseases; Pratīhārī is the monkey-faced one; Śarmakṛt cures eye ailments; Dhānyadveṣī removes poverty.
He is the virtuous one who brings happiness through his actions; he whose throat and heart possess the luster of gold;
the creator of the universe; the destroyer of the *pippala* tree; the root of hunger and the warder-off of hunger.
He whose abode is fire, the lord of the earth, whose dwelling is the earth, who takes refuge in the earth;
the king of mountains, the teacher of Dharma, the one who provides a refuge for Dharma, the supreme ruler.
Aniketa, Nimigrīva, Nīlanetra, Marutpati, Maṇimāla, Bṛhannāla, Nārada, Likuca, and Naṭa.
Kumbhāḍa, Kuṇḍalī, Cakra, Śaityakarmā, Śatākara,
Kalyāṇādhāra, Īśāna, Īśāna, and Dakṣiṇāspada.
Śatavallī, mahāvallī, cakravallī, nipānakṛt, droṇapriya, droṇarāja, gulmahṛt, and kaṭumūlaka. // Ang_1.521 //
He is eternally glorious, eternally blossoming, rootless, yet possessing many flowers;
he is born from the royal fig tree, rooted in the weapon, and fond of the night.
The Peepal tree causes great burning; it is beautiful, takes refuge on mountains, is rich in mud, is below the mud, has an excellent foundation, and is the abode of the gods.
He is the full vessel, the vessel of auspiciousness, the one made of gold, the maker of stability;
he is the glory of poetry, the bringer of fortune, the goer toward glory, the pollen that illuminates the Vedas.
Wearing a great garland, wearing a garland of living beings, rich in nooses, unbearable with his nooses, renowned as the savior of life, and beloved by the king of the gods— such is Paṇa.
He whose root is immediate, whose mind is focused on the goal, who destroys poison, who dwells among the hosts,
who resides in caves, who is the cave itself, who is the sustainer, and who is praised by the sages.
Munipriya, dantaripu, śarmakṛt, and śarmamatsarī—
these are the divine vegetables prescribed for use in the rite of ancestral offerings (śrāddha).
Through the application of acidity to these, and through the absence of that application, they indeed become twofold once again. Ang_1.528.
In the middle are the *śākuṭaka* and so forth; they should be known as threefold—by way of root, stem, and leaf—and some are distinguished by their dried state.
By means of water and oil, both separately and combined, and through the various methods of powder and paste, one should diligently prepare a thousand [preparations]. (Ang_1.530)
Having placed all of this greatness of the jackfruit tree into one vessel, the Lotus-born [Brahmā] indeed weighed it against the jackfruit itself in another vessel with his hand.
At that time, Panasa indeed became somewhat superior;
for as they looked on, she who was three hundred years old then became large.
Ginger was six hundred times [the weight of] sesame seeds, and iron was a hundred times [the weight of] ginger;
thus, these three were established upon the scale from that time forth.
On this earth, among virtuous Brahmins at a pure śrāddha rite,
a single *bṛhatkaka* of moist sesame is equal to a thousand portions of vegetables.
They diligently prepare sesame, mung beans, rice, barley, mottled beans, wheat, leafy vegetables, and other foods for the supreme satisfaction of their ancestors. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.535)
There are ten kinds of *kāśa* grasses and those *darbha* grasses considered primary and secondary;
there are ten kinds of rhinoceros meat, and [the offerings for] the *preta*, *parpaṭa*, and *bhūta* spirits.
The Brahmins such as Vāmadeva and others who specialize in the Pitṛ-sūktas, the sacred fields such as Gayā, and the banyan tree itself; Ang_1.537.
The fourteen words beginning with Bindu, Mādhava, and Viśveśa are the faces starting from Īśāna; likewise are Gadādhara and Maheśvara.
The Bhāgīrathī, the Phalgunī, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī;
all the hymns to the ancestors (pitṛsūktas), and especially those dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, others of that same kind— protective, purifying,
and specific substances for the śrāddha— are exceedingly dear to the ancestors.
All those [other trees] are but a single jackfruit tree, which causes great destruction;
yet when this jackfruit tree—the source of all one's faith—is obtained.

"On the auspicious anniversary of their death, the ancestors immediately become perpetually satisfied, well-contented, and full-bodied; such is the sacred revelation (śruti). This being so, whatever mortal here plants a jackfruit tree with a sincere heart,"
Whether with wisdom or without wisdom, or even with excessive devotion or without devotion.
Whether intentionally or even unknowingly, wherever on the surface of the earth that [person] may be, the wise declare him to be one who has performed a thousand *śrāddha* rites at Gayā. (Ang_1.544)
Having established breadfruit trees along with mangoes, plantains, and other such trees,
he diligently nurtured them according to the prescribed rites until they became auspicious.
With *campaka* trees, *pāṭalī*s, and most delightful *madhūka*s;
with *candana*, *spandana*, and *nīpa* trees, and by their shadows and their fruits.
By means of leaves, flowers, their wood, and various kinds of special vegetables,
he diligently sustained himself through his own occupation for thousands of millions of his kinsmen.
Having reached the world of Brahmā here, one shall attain union with him;
for wherever one sees a jackfruit tree, the high-minded person immediately [attains that state].
One should provide that satisfaction for the ancestors by means of wood, leaves, flowers, shoots, fruits, and so forth, or by whatever else is available. (Anga 1.549)
Immediately upon receiving that fruit from the Brahmins,
or even upon merely seeing it, one should indeed give it with devotion for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
That man who, upon seeing a jackfruit, its leaf, or its fruit,
remains silent without first offering it to satisfy his ancestors, is truly a great fool.
It is said that all his ancestors curse him in anger as soon as they see that excellent substance for drinking. (Ang_1.552)
By whatever means possible— whether by a leaf, a fruit, an unripe bud, or even by its shadow— one should act for the sake of satisfying one's ancestors.
Or whatever little one may cause to be given to those Brahmins,
by that much alone the ancestors indeed become eternally satisfied.
This being so, whatever fortunate man here, being a devotee of the Panasa tree, should constantly satisfy it with offerings out of devotion, he would become a sinner. (Ang_1.555)
Long ago, the brahmin Gālava, being hungry, saw some seeds and out of devotion purchased five or six of them to please his father.
Having himself eaten with his wife, he brought satisfaction to the ancestors;
by that alone, they too were supremely satisfied for a hundred years.
We have heard that in the past, in the holy Kuśa forest, Māṇḍavya, the most eminent knower of the Vedas, became immersed in an ocean of bliss.
On the road through the great Vindhya forest, having involuntarily seen a jackfruit tree and the sun in the month of Kārtika, he bowed silently and reflected for a moment.
Seeing those pure petals fallen upon the ground,
he, who was skillful in all tasks, carefully gathered them up.
Having quickly fashioned those leaf-cups with his own hands in haste,
he gave them to a certain son of a Brahmin who was a worthy recipient and desired water.
"How shall I drink that water which has reached the ground?"— thus he looked about even more intently as he was intent on drinking it.

Then the Great One, having remembered them, offered [the water] for the gratification of his ancestors; they too, arriving with great haste, drank it with manifold flavors. They were satisfied by that alone, even more so than by a hundred *gayā-śrāddhas*.
They immediately attained great joy toward him of such vast splendor.
Having beheld him directly and offered him excellent benedictions,
you said, "We are supremely satisfied," and thus you have achieved your great purpose.
"You are a knower of the meaning of the scriptures and the reality of the Dharma, and you have brought us complete satisfaction.
Having said this, he spoke of that state of the wielder of the discus.
As he looked on, they indeed passed before him—those who were especially to be sought after by the supreme gods; such was this great man.
The glorious Panasa, the supreme and great Vallabha, Kāra, Kāravallīka, Kāruka, Kālika, and Karut; these are the ancestors. Ang_1.568.
Then, in the presence of the gods in the Brahma-pura, these five spoke these words out of sorrow: "For indeed, this [suffering] exists for us as well."
Then there were even more thorns, harsh and very large;
O Lord, for what reason did you not make them equal to us?
Thus, afflicted by grief, they wept repeatedly and solely with extreme despondency; to them, who were in such a state, the Lord [spoke].
Again, laughing before the gods, he spoke these words:
"That you should weep for one whose greatness is so vast, whose birth was perfected, and whose splendor is supreme."
Merely unable to endure my supreme majesty upon seeing it, and desiring equality with me, you have wept from afar. (Angulimālīya-sūtra 1.573)

Therefore, from this point forward, those in the world who are poor and unable to perform even a single Śrāddha rite, even among the one hundred and eight [prescribed offerings], [should do as follows].
In certain *śrāddha* rites performed at specific times, by some means or other,
they may obtain the supreme fruit of performing the *śrāddha* through weeping.
Because you have spoken such exceedingly bitter words before me,
even while the gods were listening, therefore, in the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), you shall [be excluded]. (Angulimālīya-sūtra 1.576)
O you who are skilled in action, remain constantly joined with sourness;
O you, the *kāravallī* and others, because of your similarity to thorns! (Ang_1.577)
Since we now accept you as those whose minds are equanimous toward that [state],
you yourselves must indeed become worthy of all the funeral offerings (śrāddha).
That similarity belongs to those three alone when combined, and not individually;
it is always [the case] for a thousand vegetables such as *bṛhatī* and the like, but not for you.
By my word alone, it is understood that you possess merely the fitness for faith;
indeed, those great verses with their thorns were already present in your mind from the very beginning.
Desiring the bark of that *panasa* tree to be equal to thorns,
they remained silent after learning of this conduct of yours;
for they are exceedingly clever, highly skillful, and discerning.
Having understood his entire heart and such arrogance as it was, [he spoke].
Having understood everything, I shall act; let it be heard today throughout the worlds, concerning my own Manus and the four beginnings of the Yugas as well.

On the meritorious *aṣṭakā* days, on the transits of the sun (*saṃkrānti*), during festivals of increase (*vṛddhi*), and on occasional occasions (*naimittika*), they likewise possess such unfitness [for those rites]. (Ang 1.584)
And among these, let those that are cruel toward the rites for the deceased be directed elsewhere;
let them not exist toward others, for such a boundary has been established by me.
In that interval, there appeared a divinely created, exceedingly beautiful urvāru plant of great magnitude,
covered with leaves, flowers, large creepers, buds, and fruits.
Having arrived from the exceedingly fickle Mount Kailāsa, the supporter of the earth, he bowed with palms joined in reverence and asked: "O Earth, what is my destiny? (Ang_1.587)
Thus he spoke to the Lord Pitāmaha, the Ruler of the World,
having beheld him in such a state solely because of Gaurī’s words.
Created by Śambhu, the Lord of the World, it possesses a single, pure form;
it has come together, deeply bowed before the great gurus, and is affectionate toward them.
Perceiving him to be of pure being, free from pride, and most beautiful in every way,
the Lord spoke highly of him in the presence of the gods.
Since you were created as a pillar by Bhavānī’s word,
you are yourself great by nature— tranquil, self-controlled, and high-minded.
From this day forward on this earth, he shall be dear to his guru, humble, ever devoted to his guru,
and entirely free from pride.
In rites for the gods and for the ancestors, in auspicious and new ceremonies, in occasional, regular, and optional rites— in all of these as well.
He should always be constantly engaged and ever-ready in all specific tasks, whether involving children, the elderly, or the sick, and in all circumstances regarding unripe fruits.
May you be eternally constant throughout all the stages of the fruits of action;
may you always be the most supreme and beloved of the ancestors.
You are Vasantamādhava and Grīṣmamṛtyuñjaya;
you are Mahāvarṣā, Saptatantu, and likewise Śaratkālya.
The winter season is the king of forest groves; it is cool, refreshing, and auspicious.
It is a source of happiness, a bringer of fortune, and a constant maker of well-being.
May you become renowned among all for your auspicious drinks made from mangoes;
may you be further compared to plantains, and at times even surpassed by them.
Praised by the learned and honored by kings, may you be accepted everywhere by sixteen of your own kind, and may you be constantly beloved by all people.
At all times, existence has increased and grown excessively for everyone;
yet, through the action of the winds, beginning with the scattering of your seed, it has been further augmented.
Indeed, until the final emergence of the fruit from the seed,
it is always pure through those three intended acts and is perfected by the great mantra.
"Be the beloved of the thirty-three crores of gods!
Thus was he praised, honored, instructed, and appointed as the sinless one;
indeed, he was made the sole cause for the ultimate satisfaction of his father.
Such a person is called an *urvāru*; he is to be accepted at the rites of *śrāddha*.
There is a fault in the abandonment of *urvāru* (cucumber); indeed,
whoever out of folly should completely exclude it from the *śrāddha* rites becomes an immediate offender against his father— of this there is no doubt.
He who is an enemy of the gods, an enemy of the Vedas, and indeed an enemy of all;
he who violates the injunctions and destroys the ancestral rites—these are they whom I shall now describe.
The ninety-six occasions for ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) are proclaimed as:
the new moon, the solstices, the *dhṛti* [lunar days], the *pāta* [lunar mansions], the *mahālaya*, the three *aṣṭakās*, and the "elephant's shadow" (*gajacchāyā*). These are the ninety-six.
Those monthly śrāddhas performed thus month after month would indeed amount to one hundred and eight; these are they, and furthermore: [Ang_1.607]
The anniversary of the death of one's parents is declared to be inviolable under any circumstances;
[one should avoid it] on the first quarter of the sun (Sunday) and likewise on the second quarter of Venus (Friday).
In the third [chapter], there are thirteen [sections]; the non-explanation of the new moon (amā) is now stated.
The nature of the new moon (amāvāsya) is now clearly re-examined.
There are twelve new moon days (amāvāsyās), fourteen Manus,
four beginnings of the ages (yugādis), and twelve transits (krāntis) are traditionally taught.
There are thirteen Dhṛtis and thirteen Pātās;
fifteen Mahālayas and twelve Aṣṭakās are recorded.
Likewise, there is the single Gajacchāyā; thus, ninety-six [occasions] have been declared.
These are to be performed every month, and now all twelve of them together are proclaimed.
Indeed, one hundred and eight śrāddhas are prescribed.
Every year, with great effort, the new moon days at the end of each month were indeed fixed there for the sake of the high-souled Brāhmaṇa.
In this very context, the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) is enjoined as something that ought to be performed;
prescribed by the Śruti, it shall be the sole cause of supreme satisfaction for the ancestors.
The authors of the Smṛtis have declared this to be the archetype of all śrāddhas;
indeed, there exists no śrāddha anywhere that is superior to this one.

This very thing must be what is stated by the Śruti; for if this alone were performed, then all [rites] would be considered performed, or else [it refers to those] by whom it was performed on that same day.
"Indeed, the śrāddha is performed; they declare that this is the primordial nature (prakṛti) of all ancestral rites for others," so say the exponents of Brahman according to the Śruti.
That through whose performance all other performances arise most effectively is indeed declared as *prakṛti* by certain proponents of Brahman.
"By the performance of the Darśa-śrāddha, all śrāddhas are indeed considered performed.
Thus, all three worlds remain merely silent. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.620)
Therefore, no one abandons the supreme New Moon sacrifice (darśa);
for when this darśa has been performed by anyone in whatever manner, [the goal is attained].
"It is the established order of the world that all [duties] should be performed;
yet there, no funeral rite (*śrāddha*) is performed directly by anyone at all.
But on this earth, it is performed by some accomplished person (*kṛtin*) through whatever means."
By that very act, even if it were merely water, when performed with faith, [the goal is indeed attained].
"All these have indeed been performed"—such is the singular certainty regarding everything;
that is the vision of one who is the best of Brahmins and the practitioner of such [a path].
He alone shall be the maintainer of the sacred fire, the performer of the new-moon sacrifices, the offerer of soma, and the sacrificer of all rites; he who abandons these is a slayer of a Brahmin.
Seeing that very person— a social outcaste by his own actions, a slayer of a Brahmin,
and a sinner who has arrived— one should not honor him even with a mere word.
The *prakṛti-śrāddha* consists of the new-moon sacrifice (*darśa*) alone and nothing else;
its status as the archetype (*prakṛtitva*) is declared precisely because it is the primary form of the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*).

For this ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña), prescribed by the Vedas, is ordained for that very day; the new moon (darśa) and the annual anniversary (ābdika) are equal, and the new moon and the day of death are likewise identical, such that [the latter] can never be set aside.
If one who has renounced [the world] should abandon anything whatsoever, he falls low;
however, the anniversary of one's parents' death must be observed with food, and not otherwise.

One should not perform that [offering] with gold, food, fire-oblations, or the ritual offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) accompanied by mantras; nor with dice, grass-blades, or other mantras; nor should one do so with difficulty. Ang_1.630.
However, through the offering into the fire, the feeding of Brahmins, and the giving of funeral cakes, that rite becomes fully accomplished; otherwise, one would fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla.
The anniversary of the first year and the anniversary of the tenth year must not be omitted; likewise, the day of death and the new moon (darśa) should not be bypassed.
Indeed, by whatever means possible, these should be observed even by those who are weak.
Indeed, by those who are destitute, or weak, or especially by those who are afflicted with disease,
or by those fleeing, or even by those living incognito.

The śrāddha rite known as that for the anniversary of death cannot, under any circumstances, be omitted by those whose ritual capacity is lost, whose wealth is lost, or who are even as good as dead. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 1.634)
The day of death is determined in this manner; and every year, it must certainly be calculated according to the lunar measure itself, and not otherwise if it were not so determined.
If something were not established [by scripture], it would not be absolutely necessary;
the rule accepted by the scriptures is that there should be no repetition of what has already been established. (Ang_1.636)

The lunar days (tithis) and fires (3): 3; the lunar day and the remainder of the lunar day (1): 1; in the dark fortnight, the elephant (8), fire (3), and planets (9); the lunar day and sun (12): 12; not Śiva (11), horse (7), and the lunar day from Amā (new moon): these are recorded as the beginnings of the Manvantaras.
Therefore, they are called "arranged" (kḷpta), and for that reason they are known as "movements" (krānti);
yet, because of the sun's progression through the zodiacal signs, they are also declared to be "unarranged" (akḷpta).
The nature of the transits consists of two solstices, two equinoxes, the four *ṣaḍaśīti*s,
and the four *viṣṇupadī*s; these twelve are known as the *saṃkramaṇas*.
When the sun’s transit occurs in fixed signs, it should be known as Viṣṇupada;
when it occurs in dual-natured signs, it should be known as Ṣaḍaśītimukha.
The northern and southern solstices certainly occur when the sun enters Capricorn and Cancer; both Libra and Aries should be known as the equinoxes during the sun's transits.
Regarding the auspicious time of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti):
when the transit occurs during the day, the entire day is proclaimed to be meritorious; when the transit of the sun occurs at night, the rule for all ritual acts is as follows. [076] Ang_1.642.
Regarding the pair of northern and southern solstices, they indeed declare that there is a distinction:
having passed or not yet reached that specific time, it is proclaimed as a meritorious period.
In this way, at all transitions (saṃkrāntis), that specific time is remembered as merit-bestowing;
whichever moments are proximate to it, those are remembered as most meritorious.
The two solstices, the four equinoxes, the six "eighty" [periods],
and the four "steps of Viṣṇu"— these are remembered as the twelve transits.
In Cancer, thirty nāḍīs are prescribed; in Capricorn, twenty are recorded;
and when Libra or Aries is present, there are ten nāḍīs on both sides.
When sixty-eight [nāḍīs] have passed, sixty channels (praṇāḍikā) are said to be present;
sixteen are located before and sixteen after the meritorious Viṣṇupadī.
If the transit occurs at midnight or after it, during the southern course of the sun, one should perform the rite on the preceding day;
however, during the northern course, one should indeed do so on that very day.

In a *śrāddha* performed with food, the *kutapa* [period] applies; for whatever ancestral rite (*paitṛka-karma*) is performed with food, that indeed should be done during the *kutapa*. But if it is different from that, then this [following rule] applies.
There is no doubt that this procedure for the mere *odana-śrāddha* and for all the *saṃkrāntis* has been proclaimed by the eternal knowers of Dharma. (Ang 1.650)
Among those twelve others as well, the *kutapa* is said to be the foremost;
they are prescribed for bathing, giving, libations, and other such rites performed apart from that [specific time].
Although these specific times have been prescribed for various occasions,
for the skillful performer of the *śrāddha*, every time is the right time.
The Kutapa is declared by the words of the Vedas to be the primary [time], and not any other;
it is that day on which the period of the sun’s southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is correctly present.
One should perform it during the northern course of the sun, for indeed the northern course is auspicious;
however, wherever the Kutapa hour may occur, one should act with that as the primary consideration.

Just as one would perform all the śrāddha rites for the new moon, the sun’s transits (saṃkrānti), and so forth— including the śrāddhas for the two transits— so too should one properly perform them during this Kutapa period in the northern course of the sun.
The wise have declared that these are merely transpositions and not actual arrangements;
likewise, *dhṛti* and *pāta* are numbered at twenty-six.
It is said that all [these] were indeed left unestablished;
there are many kinds of Mahālayas, namely fifteen in number from of old.
Some say there are sixteen [links], others likewise say ten;
some say five, three, or even just one. (Ang_1.658)
The virtuous have declared those [Aṣṭakās] to be sixfold, while twelve are traditionally recorded;
this occurs when the moon is in the constellation sacred to the ancestors (Maghā) and the sun is situated in Hasta.
When the lunar day (tithi) falls under the constellation of Yama, it is proclaimed as Gajacchāyā;
what are the rites for the ancestors (śrāddhadevatāḥ), and which are known as those pertaining solely to the three deities?
What are the six deities, and what are the nine deities?
First of all, that which has three deities is said to be the single day of death.
The Darśa sacrifice has six deities, while the Aṣṭakās have nine deities;
[these rites should be performed] during the Aṣṭakās, at a time of prosperity, at Gayā, and on the anniversary of a death.
One should perform the śrāddha for one's mother separately, except when it is performed together with the father;
if it is performed separately from the father, it must be done together with him.
That would create an obstacle to the happiness of his great paternal kinship;
first comes the group of paternal ancestors, and after that, the group of maternal ancestors.
Then follows this group for the maternal grandfathers along with their wives;
at the rite for the ancestors, it is performed counter-clockwise,
and the forehead is left bare.
Where the group of ancestors is first, there the circumambulation should be counter-clockwise.
Likewise, the forehead may become empty;
wherever there is the left-turning [of the hair], in that very place there is the counter-clockwise direction.
Likewise, it is remembered that the forehead and the principal limbs are empty;
where these three are located, no house-decoration should be performed, for there is no house-decoration in those places.
Regarding the circumambulation and other rites for the group of Mothers: one should perform the circumambulation starting from where the group of Mothers is located first;
likewise, the auspicious mark on the forehead should be on the left side, as should the auspicious bath.
Furthermore, the decoration of the home and auspicious rites,
as well as the sequential order for the ancestors, must be maintained constantly.

It should begin with the great-grandfather, have the grandfather in the middle, and end with the father; this is declared to be the characteristic of its recitation. According to the different types of *śrāddha*, the Viśvedevas [are invoked].
And their Viśvedevas are named Satya;
furthermore, the word *vṛddha* should be employed everywhere in all four [of these cases].
In the same way, regarding the group of mothers and the third group as well, this recitation of theirs should occur according to the order of birth.
All that which is contrary to this is contrary to it; this supreme [teaching] should be understood as being entirely so—indeed, all those deities are thus.
In this context, the Vasus are the fathers, the Rudras are the grandfathers, and the Ādityas are declared to be the great-grandfathers; these are their respective groups.

The wise have declared that the performance of the single Śrāddha known as *pātheya* (provision for the journey) is prescribed for the fourth ancestor who precedes these three, for the purpose of defining *sāpiṇḍya*.
Thus, this has been the definition of sapinda-relationship known as extending to seven ancestors;
and impurity (āśauca) is proclaimed to last ten days, three days, or one day, and all such birth-impurity (sūtaka) is declared to apply to their descendants.

Furthermore, there are those known as *samānodaka* (distant sapindas) and those who share the same lineage (*sagotra*); beyond them, it should be understood that the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for them is as follows.
It is taught that one should bathe for three days and then one day;
this sequence continues in this manner until the very end.
This has been described merely as a ritual bath, mentioned here incidentally;
however, that which is called the "living śrāddha" (jīvacchrāddha) is said to be distinct from all other forms of śrāddha.
It consists of forty deities, or else it is joined again with a number of five;
therefore, they say that it is remembered as being of two kinds.
Furthermore, some *śrāddhas* are accompanied by deities, while others are not; these are now being described.
The *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the *gayā-śrāddha*, likewise the *hata-śrāddha*,
the *dadhi-śrāddha*, the *tṛṇa-śrāddha*, and all others beginning with *amā* [the new moon].
All śrāddha rites for the departed (preta-śrāddha) are declared to be accompanied by offerings to the gods;
it is taught that all those [rites] involving the water-pot (udakumbha) are without offerings to the gods.
In the *amāśrāddha* (new moon śrāddha) and in all *pretaśrāddhas*, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is traditionally considered the primary requirement; furthermore,
the granting of permission (*abhyanujñā*) is also highly esteemed in this context.
This is considered the vehicle. Ang_1.684
Having prepared the water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), along with perfumes, incense, lamps, and flowers—
either individually or all together— and sesame seeds, one should perform everything silently, except for the recitation of the entire Veda.
In that regard, worship should be performed, as well as the offering of funeral cakes and a sacrificial fee;
here, curd, clarified butter, and indeed clothing are essential and supreme.
One should perform it only in the forenoon; one should not look toward the *kutapa* cloth.
One should offer the rice balls (*piṇḍas*) to crows or vultures;
if not, one should offer them to aquatic creatures, but one must not cast them elsewhere.
Those entitled to perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite are the brother, the sister, the son, the master, and the maternal uncle.
For a friend, a teacher, a father, a mother, a sister,
as well as for a father-in-law and a brother-in-law, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is prescribed, not the *pārvaṇa*.

There are śrāddhas both with rice-balls (piṇḍa) and without rice-balls; likewise, the śrāddha performed at the time of the sun’s transit between signs (yugakrānti), the śrāddha for the deceased (preta-śrāddha), and so forth.
Those known as "without rice-balls" are [specific], while the others are "with rice-balls."
If there were sixteen Mahālayas, the Gajacchāyā would not occur here;
for that [Gajacchāyā] exists because of the number fifteen, in order to reach the total count of ninety-six.
By whichever enumeration— that is, by that sixfold method—
there may be the accomplishment of the state of being the Great Abode (mahālaya), and likewise the specific fruit [is attained].
In every case, it is thus declared that from an increase in effort, a very great fruit indeed arises; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
The Mahālaya, the Mahālaya— this is proclaimed to be twofold, occurring on fortnightly occasions; indeed,
it is distinguished therein by whether it involves a single Brahmin or multiple Brahmins.
First, I shall describe the nature of the position known as the "single Brahmin," which pertains solely to all those belonging to the Mahālaya school until the end of their faction.
Those who were selected on the first day, or those of others exclusively, they alone—
and no others— should be appointed at the end of the fortnight for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of the śrāddha.
For it should be given only once, and not at various times;
however, O Brahmins, when there is a multitude of brahmins, it may be given perpetually.
They should be performed individually and separately at every moment,
and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be bestowed separately for each person.
If the Brahmins are not to be chosen individually for each group according to the rule,
then in every case they should belong to six deities or indeed to nine deities.
The Great Lay (mahālaya) is renowned by the virtuous as being sixfold;
it should be performed in this very manner, and one should not practice it otherwise.
If one should perform the Mahālaya rite once, specifically with various deities,
that indeed is the "once-performed Mahālaya," and it is thus remembered as such.
A certain supreme and great rite has been described as equal to the *śrāddha* at Gayā;
it is an extraordinary *mahāśrāddha* that cannot be fully defined by any of the scriptures.
Even such a performer of the śrāddha rite [should do so] joined with the six deities,
or even with the nine deities, or accompanied by Viṣṇu.
One should perform the Mahālaya śrāddha joined with Dhūrilocana,
either once within a fortnight or on whichever of the previously mentioned occasions is appropriate.
If one should perform it for even a single fortnight, he becomes a performer of the Mahālaya rite;
indeed, there is no other śrāddha that is equal to this Gayā-śrāddha.
"One must certainly perform this specific meritorious *śrāddha*"; such is the sacred revelation (*śruti*).
Regarding the excellence of the *mahālaya*, the *bharaṇī* constellation, and so forth:
day by day it is equal to Gayā; on the *bharaṇī* day, the "five-fold Gayā" (*gayapañcaka*) is attained.
Tenfold the merit is on a Vyatīpāta day; twentyfold in the middle of the fortnight;
they say it is a hundredfold on the twelfth lunar day, but a thousandfold on the new moon day.
The period of Mahālaya begins with the full moon of Āṣāḍha; its fifth fortnight is declared to be Mahālaya for the successful performance of Śrāddha rites for the ancestors.
The Mahālaya [rite] for ascetics is performed there; specifically, one should perform the Śrāddha for ascetics on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) for those who have died an untimely death.
On the fourteenth day, one should especially perform rites for those who have died an untimely death.
It is declared that on the ninth day, a single *śrāddha* rite for those who are auspicious should be performed for those women who are auspicious,
until such time as their husbands remain alive— even if they are the wives of those who do not maintain the Vedic scriptures.
Therefore, in the world of living beings, one may or may not perform both of these;
for this is the practice when the Mahālaya rite is performed only once.
As long as the paternal dharmas persist, he is considered by him to be equal;
but if that side has passed away, then he is distinct from the other side.
In another such case, or likewise in another of that kind,
one should continue to practice that [remedy] for as long as the scorpion remains;
once the scorpion has become invisible, its father is the ultimate [cause].
When the month of Dhanus has arrived, indeed observing the non-performance of the śrāddha rite;
Indeed, they become intent on bestowing curses immediately;
therefore, one should with devotion perform the Śrāddha ceremony known as Mahālaya at that very time.
One should perform it according to the prescribed rule; otherwise, a great fault would arise.
Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should perform at least a single *śrāddha*.

One should indeed perform [the rite] every year, equal to the *śrāddha* for one's father; on the following day of the *mahālaya*, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed. All the annual duties are fulfilled by that single performance of the *mahālaya*.
Therefore, the libation (tarpaṇa) should indeed take place on the following day;
on that subsequent day, one should worship as many [deities] as were designated for the śrāddha.
The libation (tarpaṇa) is performed before sunrise;
with the sesame seeds and darbha grass remaining from that [ancestral rite], one who has lost his paternal ancestors is indeed authorized to perform this libation prior to the rising of the sun.
He whose offspring have perished shall always be entitled to perform the libation (tarpaṇa);
likewise, one whose father is living shall constantly perform the śrāddha for the monthly ancestral rites, the pitṛyajña, and the nāndīśrāddha.

The performer [of the rite] should be a living being; until the oblation is offered, it is traditionally considered an instrument. However, in the first two cases, the *nāndī-śrāddha* must always be performed at all times.
A son should give to those very same persons to whom his father would have given;
this applies when the father has fallen from his status, has renounced the world, is diseased, or is afflicted solely by illness.
A son should perform that paternal rite which is his duty;
at the *śrāddha*, he has the right to offer for his parents who maintain the Vedic fires, as well as for his own wife and his mother-in-law. (Anga 1.723)
The Śrāddha for one's maternal grandfather and his wife should be performed in the domestic fire (aupāsana);
however, for all others, the Śrāddha should be performed in the common fire (laukikānala).
For paternal uncles, brothers, and elder siblings who are childless,
as well as for all their wives, [the cremation] shall be performed according to the prescribed rule in the worldly fire (laukikāgni).
It must be performed as an obligatory duty and not abandoned by anyone according to the Dharma;
it should consist of at least the annual Śrāddha, equal in nature to the ancestral Śrāddha for one's father.
Regarding the *aṣṭakā*, the monthly *śrāddha*,
and the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha: on whichever night one performs the fire-oblation (*homa*) with mantras, one should then offer a handful of curd in place of the cake (*apūpa*).
Then, on the ninth day, one should perform a śrāddha with devotion according to the prescribed rule;
however, it may be performed merely by means of the procedure for the monthly śrāddha.
Indeed, all those remaining eleven Aṣṭakās must surely have been performed;
this is said to be a concise method.
Just as all ancestral rites are considered as good as performed by means of the *darśa* śrāddha on the *aṣṭakā* days, so too has this light means been proclaimed.
All these rites must indeed be performed separately according to the rule;
they are known as one hundred and eight, though sometimes there are specific variations.
But for one who is incapable, some easy means has been prescribed;
however, a twice-born man who is capable should perform it according to the ritual every year. [086] Ang_1.732 //
One should perform all the śrāddha rites; if one does not, a fault is proclaimed.
Now, the entire procedure for the śrāddha and the application of the śrāddha are being fully described by me.
The invitation and the formal summons must be performed according to the prescribed rules on the preceding day;
these are the persons worthy of being invited.
This must always be performed by those Brahmins who possess Vedic knowledge, and certainly not by those who lack it.
The food of those who remains in the stomach is digested through the study of the Vedas;
they rescue their lineage—ten ancestors and ten descendants.
But that Brahmin who studies the Vedas, who is constantly established in the Brahman,
who is of good conduct and maintains the sacred fire— he indeed is Agni Kavyavāhana.
If one invites those devoid of Vedic knowledge and offers a śrāddha purified by mantras to one who is mantra-less,
that food remains within his stomach and weeps; of this there is no doubt.
That food indeed curses its giver with such a fate; it curses the giver of the sacrifice and that very food which resides within his heart. (Ang 1.738)
For as many morsels of sacrificial oblation as that glutton consumes,
for so many pikes does he swallow upon reaching Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
They cut off the hand of the donor and the tongue of the other; they gouge out the eyes of the one who sees and the pair of ears of the one who hears.
When one's own Vedic branch is difficult to find, one should offer food to those who belong to other branches; however,
one belonging to one's own branch is praiseworthy,
and especially at a *śrāddha* for one's parents, one should offer food to those of one's own branch.
The giving away of a daughter, the ancestral śrāddha rite, and that which is to be bestowed with effort should be given only to those of pure conduct, and certainly not to those of impure conduct.

Those who are afflicted by disease, those of corrupt intellect, those intent on wicked conduct, those full of faults and hatred, those with deformed nails, and those with blackened teeth are unfit to be fed.
He will be eternally one whose body lacks vigor, ill-colored, and misshapen;
he will live by the stars, perform the work of a slave, and subsist solely on the labor of Śūdras.
One who has a single Śūdra as his officiating priest, one nourished by a Śūdra, one whose home is a Śūdra’s,
one intent on receiving gifts from a Śūdra, and one who is constantly a beggar.
Likewise, one who is fickle, cruel, self-conceited, prone to cursing, excessively proud, ungraspable, inactive, and a reviler of the Vedas; ||| Ang_1.746 |||
One who constantly sells the Vedas, a village priest,
one who hates the Veda, and one intent on seizing the property of a Brahmin— [these should be avoided].
One who is devoted to another's wife, the wicked one who thinks only of another's wife,
he who has abandoned his own wife, he who has given away his son, and likewise he who sells his son.

One who harms his mother or father, one who betrays his teacher, one whose mind is intent on amassing wealth, a wealthy man who is harsh, one who is merciless, one who is averse to giving, an atheist, and one who reviles others— [these are those with whom one should not associate].
Jewelers, goldsmiths, dyers, and so forth, as well as priests.
One who is excessively conceited, insatiable, prone to harsh speech, hypocritical, and dull-witted;
one who, having abandoned the Vedic rites, exerts effort solely in the study of other scriptures.

One who is an atheist, one who is concerned with what will happen in the future, one who is a debtor, one who has abandoned the Vedas, one who has abandoned ritual bathing, one who has abandoned the twilight devotions, and one who has ceased the practice of shaving.
One who has had half of his hair shaved, one who is insignificant, one with an enlarged penis,
one who is worthless, one who is hunchbacked, as well as one who is blind, deaf, deluded, or excessively coarse.

One who is insane, weak, exhausted, angry, or has deformed nails; one who is addicted to pleasure, a son of an adulteress, a son of an unmarried woman, an outcast, impure, or born from another's childbirth.
One who subsists on the food of others, one who is dependent on others, a farmer, a usurer, a bull,
one who follows the livelihood of a king, one who follows the livelihood of a Vaiśya, one who follows the livelihood of a Śūdra, and one who is evil-minded.

One who is extremely fickle, one who is exhausted, one whose husband is not a hero, likewise one whose protector is pregnant, one whose food is unfit to be eaten, and one who is difficult to approach.
One who is the son of a non-Vedic scholar, one who wears the clothes of an artisan, one who is wicked and treacherous,
a singer, one with sores, one who speaks meanly, and one who speaks trivially.
One who causes laughter, an actor skilled in the art of drama,
a man of lowly deeds, a creature of trivial life, one who lives by his labor, and one who lives on a permanent salary.
One should not, with great effort, feed [the preceptor] after the day of invitation; having avoided three days, one should choose [him] through the practice of "excessive conduct" (*aticaryā*).
One should abandon a recipient who eats every month for a period of only a fortnight.
One should abandon for a full month a person who eats during the deficient fortnight.
In the case of a *nagna-śrāddha*, [the period of impurity] lasts for one year; in the case of a *nava-śrāddha*, half of that;
in the sixteenth [monthly rite], one and a half years; and in the *sapiṇḍana* rite, two years.
Having excluded the twice-born, one should subsequently cause them to undertake the rite of *śrāddha*;
likewise, one should properly abandon a Śūdra who attends a *śrāddha* for three years.
One should constantly and thoroughly avoid for a full year the consumption of food from the śrāddha rites of kings or vaiśyas,
as well as the work of village outcasts.
On that day, one should not look upon the recipient of the *āmaśrāddha*;
the domestic priest (*purohita*) of the Divākīrtis is not to be spoken to by day or by night.
On auspicious days, the family priest of the potters must never be spoken to,
especially on Sundays, Tuesdays, and Fridays.
One should carefully avoid conversing with the domestic priest of another,
nor with the priests of twice-born men or courtesans on the days of the lunar festivals and during the times of planetary conjunctions.
Indeed, these [objects] are not to be regarded at all; for whenever they are seen, one achieves the fulfillment of all duties simply by reciting the *anuvāka* on fire. (Ang 1.767)
If one who accepts gifts at sacred fords (tīrtha) is seen on the day of a śrāddha, as well as one who lives by those fords, a resident there, or even the priest of such a place; 1.768.
When he has been seen, one should look up, thinking, "May we see the sun. This is the concealment;
it is for one whose account of the conduct of the Three Sages is most clearly manifest. (Ang. 1.769)
One who is thus disciplined, free from darkness, devoid of greed and hypocrisy,
content with whatever is obtained by chance, learned in the Vedas, wise, and pure— [to such a one should one give].
Therefore, one should [entrust] a twice-born man who maintains the perpetual fire, is of mature age, wise, born of a noble family, free from any desire for recompense, and pleasant of countenance.
Having carefully examined [the guest], one should properly choose a Brahmin for the śrāddha rite;
first, being self-restrained and holding a pavitra in hand, one should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
Holding *darbha* grass in his hand, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), moving very slowly,
free from anger and with a pleasant countenance, he should perform his formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with speech.
Having proclaimed the place and the time, as well as the subject matter,
one should then designate the ordinary ancestors and gods, and likewise perform the ordinary rite.

One should first form the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), thinking, "I shall perform the ritual act. For the sake of propitiating all the Viśvedevas, one should offer *darbha* grass; their place here is in the Āhavanīya fire.
"Having granted a moment, let favor be shown today; this is what is proclaimed.
Thus, one should indeed place *darbha* grasses in the right hand of the twice-born.
This indeed is declared to be the invitation (varaṇa) for the ancestors;
having performed the worship of the mandala, the invitation follows, when it is said, "Oṃ, so be it."
Having prepared a pure mandala according to the ritual rules using cow dung,
one should first worship the mandala dedicated to the gods and that dedicated to the ancestors.
When the Brahmin has been welcomed on the western side of the mandala,
one should offer him water for his feet right there and wash them over the mandala.
Washing below the ankles during the *śrāddha* rite for the washing of the feet would be preferable;
for by water adhering to the hair on the feet, the ancestors fall into a terrible hell. (Ang 1.780)
If there should be hair clinging [to the feet] during the washing of the feet,
one should wash them at most up to the knees in order to avoid that fault.

The section on sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed for six occasions: at the beginning and at the end, during the offering of water for the feet (pādya), upon the seat (viṣṭara), during the scattering of grain (vikira), and when giving the rice-ball for the remnants (ucchiṣṭapiṇḍa). Ang_1.782.
If the preparer has already rinsed his mouth while the eater has not yet done so, and the eater nevertheless performs the act of rinsing,
that water is equal to the urine of a dog; therefore, one should avoid it.
Facing north, one should offer food and so forth for the gods, and facing south for the ancestors;
at the pārvaṇa rite, one should present everything according to the prescribed procedure for the worship of the gods.
Some say the time for the three offerings is on the preceding day at night, on that very day at dawn,
and again on that day during the Kutapa period; thus they declare the Śrāddha should be performed three times.
Out of weariness with that [repetition], they perform the śrāddha only once;
having performed the formal invitation (varaṇa) in its place, they perform the entire śrāddha rite.

Then, with the mantra ending in "svāhā," namely "oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā," he should likewise offer the seat (*viṣṭara*) with the words, "This is your seat; [O ancestors], this is your seat. (AngS 1.787)
The word *svadhā* is prescribed in every instance in the place of the ancestors;
by this very mantra, their supreme worship is ordained.
For this is the supreme and great mantra for the worship of the ancestors;
it should be employed on the day of the śrāddha, whereas other mantras are merely ordinary syllables.
Having addressed all the gods and the ancestors by name,
and thereafter, one should offer a seat using the very mantra previously mentioned.
One should offer a seat using the word ending in the genitive case, saying, "Please be seated for a moment.
One should grant the moment [of rest] by means of a blade of *darbha* grass or by touching the hand.
And you, sirs, should attain [the goal]; one should indeed speak with "Tāra" as the prefix.
Having prepared the *arghya* offering, if it has been performed, it is declared that it must be performed again. Thus it is said. 1.792.
Having spread *darbha* grass upon the surface of the earth, one should place there an inverted vessel,
and then cover it over with *darbha* grass.
Having lifted it up and sprinkled it, one should place barley into that vessel along with *śambara* incense;
then, having first offered *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, as well as perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, and so forth,
and having placed those into the water, one should cause the *arghya* offering to be presented into his hand.
The invocation may precede that [offering], or it may follow; it is optional.
If he has the intention to perform [the rite], then he should proceed with the *vyāhṛti*s;
or else, saying "The divine ones... (*yā divyā*), or "O gods, this is for you" (*devā vo 'rdhyam*). (Ang_1.796)
One should indeed offer that *arghya* to the gods and the ancestors in due order;
at the invocation, the Viśvedevas are addressed with the pair of verses beginning with "uśantas tvā."
It is proclaimed in both places that some [recite] one verse here as "viśve devāsaḥ," while others recite the subsequent one as "viśve devāḥ. (Ang. 1.798)
They indeed recite for the sake of the gods, "May they come," and likewise at the station of the ancestors, "Desiring you, may they come to us."
Some might say that this [which has been stated] is the supreme [truth] here;
however, what has been explained as "done" or "not done" is not intended to invalidate what has not been explicitly mentioned.
However, because the mere Vedic mantras are not recited, [one should offer] perfumes, unbroken rice, barley, and so forth;
incense, lamps, fine silk, and all such items, as well as the sacred thread.
One should give everything with the ritual formulas or silently, according to one's preference; then,
if it has not been performed previously according to one's own Sūtra, one should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) in the fire.
Furthermore, some of those actions may have been performed without the recitation of mantras;
this is because they exceed the scope of the ritual action previously undertaken through formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
This concludes the section on formal resolve.
That [intention] becomes doubled;
indeed, through that very doubling, one should again form a resolution and perform the ritual action preceded by it.
One should understand it thus in all cases regarding those various acts of volition;
for otherwise, the volition of a single person would indeed become manifold at once.
Indeed, until the completion of the procedure for the ancestral rite (*paitṛka*) at hand,
one should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) again by reciting the unspoken mantras.
If an action proceeds on dry land by the mere utterance of a mantra, then indeed,
no further volition can prevail within that action.
Therefore, having first formed a mental resolve, one should then begin the preparation;
having strewn those *darbha* grasses according to the rule with their tips pointing toward the south, one should attend to the sequence of the manner of serving the food.
Having taken cooked food and spread a base [of ghee] once more,

"Svadhā! Homage! I satisfy the father and the grandfather."
Having likewise performed the śrāddha for the great-grandfather and the others beginning with the Vasus, each joined by their respective name and lineage, and thereafter—

Thus ends the Āṅgirasa [section].
