Chapter Two:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the characteristics of *upasthāna* (attendance upon the sacred fire).
For one who has approached according to the proper rule deserves the instruction of the vows.
A wicked person who is certain [of his sin] should not eat immediately upon arriving;
for by eating while present in such an assembly, he increases his evil.
In a state of doubt, one must not eat until the matter has been definitively resolved;
likewise, one should act only according to authoritative means of knowledge until the formal instruction is received.
Having committed a sin, one should not conceal it; for if it is concealed, it increases.
Whether it be small or great, one should confess it to those who know the Dharma.
For they are physicians for those who have committed evil and diagnosticians of sins,
just as skilled physicians are for those afflicted by disease.
When an occasion for expiation has arisen, a venerable twice-born man who is devoted to truth, gentle, and endowed with uprightness should always seek purification;
having bathed with his clothes on, restrained in speech, wearing wet garments, and composed in mind.
Whether he be a kṣatriya or a vaiśya, he should then approach the assembly.
Then, being in pain, he quickly went to the ground for prostration;
with his limbs and his head, he did not utter a single word.
Then, having seen him approach and having seated him on an auspicious seat, those brahmins, observing his prostration, asked what his purpose was.
"What is your business, or for what purpose have you come, O twice-born one? Or what do you seek?
Speak all that in this assembly—whatever task is for your own benefit."
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Attendance upon the Assembly," in the *Āṅgirasa-dharmaśāstra*.
The third chapter:
By truth the king shines; by truth the sun shines.
Fire shines by means of truth; everything is established upon truth.
The three worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar—are established in truth;
for all of us as well, truth alone is the supreme goal.
If one speaks the truth, happiness will certainly be attained.
For one who is grasped by the unreal shall never be purified.
"Men who desire purity are purified by truth alone;
therefore, speak that which is the truth, from beginning to middle to end."
Thus authorized by them, one should speak the truth in its entirety;
once that matter has been reported, the litigant should be dismissed.
Once that evil person has been expelled, those reciters of the Dharma should deliberate there accordingly,
consulting with one another.
That which is proclaimed in the teachings of the authoritative ones, that which is accompanied by compassion,
the excellence of the assembly, and the relative strength and weakness of actions.
Having considered the place, the time, and whatever other circumstances may exist, as well as the entire assembly, one should prescribe the penance.
Whatever is certain for all and whatever does not cause the loss of life,
that one person appointed by the assembly should be summoned and made to hear it.
Listen, O Brahmin, to this vow that is being enjoined upon you;
it must be performed with diligent effort, otherwise it will be in vain for you. (Ang_2.3.10)
And when their practice has been completed, then the proclamation of purification should be performed with every effort; it is not to be honored by Brahmins according to one's own power alone.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Ordinance of Expiation," in the *Āṅgirasa-dharmaśāstra*.
Chapter Four:
"Prāya" is said to be austerity (*tapas*), and "citta" is called determination (*niścaya*).
Through the application of ascetic resolve, it is traditionally taught that this constitutes expiation.
Having caused the mind to undergo a process equal to the penance, that which is performed by the assembly is traditionally known as *prāyaścitta* (atonement). // Ang_2,4.2 //

Whether they be four or even three, those Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Agnihotra sacrifice, who are firmly established in righteousness and have discerned what ought and ought not to be done.
These seven are proclaimed as the formulators of penances,
together with twenty-one others who have attained the status of attendants.

Even a single person may constitute an assembly [for the purpose of adjudicating dharma] if he is a twice-born who has fulfilled his Vedic vows with the *sāvitrī* as his sole essence; or if he is an ascetic (*yatī*) who knows the self through knowledge, a meditator who realizes the self; or one who has performed the *śirovratas* and completed his ritual ablutions (*snātaka*). *Angulimālīya Sūtra* 2.4.5.
Thus, it was previously stated by me that among those who are each progressively higher,
those who are content with their own specific function are designated as belonging to the assembly.
For these [beings], the [wisdom] is middling in regard to minor and middling tasks,
and it is even hundreds of times more so, or indeed further still, in regard to reflections on the great transgressions.
But beyond this, those brahmins who are merely bearers of the name do not possess the status of an assembly, even if they number in the thousands.
Brahminhood is established through birth, physical form, knowledge, conduct, sacred learning, and dharma as it has been described.
Just as a painting is gradually brought to completion by means of many constituent parts, so too is this status attained.
In the same way, the status of a Brahmin would also arise through the purificatory rites preceded by mantras.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Assembly," in the *Āṅgirasa-dharmaśāstra*.
The fifth chapter begins:
One who is learned in the four Vedas, one who is skilled in the ritual alternatives (*vikalpī*), one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgavid*), and one who recites the Dharma.
And the three principal stages of life—this assembly consists of at least ten such members.
Those best of the twice-born who have mastered all four Vedas are remembered as "Cāturvedyas," even if they lack their respective auxiliary sciences (aṅgas).
That twice-born man who knows the authoritative standard for these three— the Dharma, the assembly, and the sequence of penance— shall be the one empowered to make the legal determination.
One should become a knower of the auxiliary sciences (aṅgavid) through certainty in grammar, Vedic meter, ritual procedure, phonetics, astronomy, and etymology. Ang_2,5.4.
One who has completed the ceremonial bath after mastering the Vedas and their branches, who is endowed with noble lineage and good conduct,
and who knows many treatises on dharma, is recited as a "reciter of dharma" (dharmapāṭhaka).
After the stage of the religious student (*brahmacarya-āśrama*), one is called "venerable" (*vṛddha*) upon reaching the next stage of life.
Among those very venerable persons who have been thus described,
the assembly of Brahmins is declared to be twice as large as that of kings.
For Vaiśyas, the assembly is indeed threefold, and the vow is likewise prescribed.
A Brāhmaṇa among Brāhmaṇas, a reciter among Kṣatriyas,
and one who is an interrogator among Vaiśyas— these alone are recorded as the givers of vows.
But for one who officiates at the sacrifices of Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas,
having prescribed the penance, he should perform the Taptakṛcchra.
Having thus indicated the views among the castes, beginning with the Kṣatriyas,
I shall now describe the unsurpassed atonement for those who have engaged in [forbidden acts].
A Śūdra devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins shall be purified in due time;
likewise, one devoted to the service of the twice-born may be purified by gifts or by fasts.
Alternatively, for one who abides by the duties of a Kṣatriya while taking recourse to the path,
having first made him a Brāhmaṇa in the interim, one should then prescribe his vow.
Therefore, having encountered a Śūdra who stands upon the path of dharma,
one should grant him an expiation that is devoid of Vedic dharma;
or rather, whatever dharma or vow by which he has fallen into distress may satisfy him.
For indeed, by the grace of the brahmins, everyone may be delivered.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Regulation of Penances," in the *Āṅgirasa-dharmaśāstra*.
The sixth chapter [begins]: "In the case of a fine, however, the strength of the assembly (*pariṣad*) is the authority for the procedure of the assembly."
And he also attended upon those who performed meritorious deeds, and his strength was correctly reported [to him].
Where there is no assembly, or where the assembly is improper,
or where the task is otherwise stated, purity is difficult for him to attain there.
The assembly should be conducted according to the rules so that all members become more powerful;
in such a way, no evil enters into that union.
Having attained this and its application in such a manner, one perishes,
just as a small amount of salt is dissolved when thrown into a great body of water.
For one whose primary focus is this yoga, all activities should be purified;
that substance [is purified] through contact with the ear, just as the purification of the mouths [is achieved by the breath]. Ang_2.6.5.
Whatever sin belongs to the perpetrator who is being pacified through dharma according to the scriptures, that [sin] departs entirely; I shall explain this to you part by part.
The teacher is the instructor for those who possess self-control; the king is the instructor for the wicked;
and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the instructor for those whose sins are concealed within.
Whether it be a teacher, a king, or even a judge, one is bound by the law;
yet the teacher is liberated from evil, having struck away fear through virtue.
When the penance has been performed and the Brahmin’s sin has been burnt away, I ask you about Dharma in its true essence: where, then, does that evil reside?
It does not go to the agent, nor does it go to the retinue;
through the conjunction of wind and the rays of the sun, it dissolves completely like water.
Burnt by the three sacrificial fires of that wise purifier, they perish;
of this there is no doubt, just as frost vanishes before the sight of the sun.
Whatever one might say from a partisan standpoint, or whatever is outside the assembly—
both those fools go to hell because of that action.
He who speaks while not knowing, or he who speaks otherwise even while knowing—
there is indeed fault for both of them in both positions.
For those who do not know [the truth], there is the fault of giving; for those who know, there is the fault of not giving.
Such would be a great fault; therefore, one should always speak after having understood.
But that expiation which is offered by those who have assembled without knowing [the rules],
that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon the giver alone.
But those Brahmins who are correctly established, having mastered the Dharma and the Vedāṅgas,
are capable of delivering them and of bestowing grace upon themselves.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Expiatory Rites and Conduct," in the *Āṅgirasa-dharmaśāstra*.
The seventh chapter:
Regarding those twice-born men who seek expiatory rites for those who are afflicted...
Those who, though knowing [the truth], do not bestow it, go together with them.
Therefore, having encountered one who is afflicted, and especially a Brahmin,
those who know the path of the assembly must not turn their backs and abandon it.
The expiation must be declared;

for the sake of establishing the authority of the rite, the instructors should prescribe the vow either sequentially or in its entirety, even if [the transgression] was committed unknowingly. Ang_2,7.3 //
If someone should rescue from fear a Brahmin who is afflicted by fear anywhere,
by thus lifting him out of evil, he shall obtain a fruit equal to that [of the former].
Penance must not be granted by twice-born men, even if they possess knowledge, unless it is requested, offered, or asked for according to the prescribed rule. [139] Ang_2,7.5 //
Therefore, people should give after having obtained the permission of the assembly;
nor [should they give] while others are talking, for in this way the Dharma is not lost.
For grave sins, the assembly consists of one hundred; for major sins such as the *mahāpātakas*, it is one thousand;
for secondary sins (*upapāpaka*), it is fifty; and for minor offenses, it is a small number—this is the settled rule.
The five who commit the great sins are:
the slayer of a Brahmin, the stealer of gold, the drinker of intoxicants, and the violator of the Guru’s bed;
and the fifth is anyone else who associates with these outcasts.
The killer of a woman or a man, the defiler of a maiden, and the stealer of cows—
these four are declared to be outcasts (patita), just like the slayer of a Brahmin and others.
Minor offenses (upapātaka), however, are innumerable, and they include such acts as the killing of a cow and so forth.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Enumeration of Sins," in the *Āṅgirasadharmaśāstra*.
The eighth chapter concerns the acceptance of gifts (*pratigraha*).
But that brahmin who maintains the sacred fires yet accepts gifts from a Śūdra attains equality with those who consume such food and goes to the womb of an animal. (Ang_2.8.1)
He who, while studying the Veda, eats the food of a Śūdra,
attains the fruit of the Veda for the Śūdra and himself descends to the state of a Śūdra. (Angiras 2.8.2)
Having praised a Śūdra,
and having smelled, drunk, looked upon, touched, or accepted [something from him],
one who says "Praise him" and "May it be well," is indeed an eater [of that food]; of this there is no doubt.
These are the faults that arise here from accepting the food of a Śūdra;
however, I shall now declare the favor permitted by Manu in ancient times.
Whether it be raw or cooked, if one partakes of the food of a Śūdra, the eater incurs the guilt; and so does the Brahmin who serves as his domestic priest.
Having accepted [food], one should give it to others—
especially to teachers, the sacred fire, guests, and dependents; having accepted it, it should be given away, and one should not eat it oneself.
For one who constantly studies while nourished by the food of a Śūdra, or for one who recites prayers or offers oblations while nourished by the food of a Śūdra, there is no higher destination.
If one eats the food of a Śūdra continuously for six months, and then for another six months,
he becomes a Śūdra even while alive; once dead, he is reborn as a dog.
If a twice-born man, especially one who has maintained the sacred fires, dies after having eaten the food of a Śūdra without first performing atonement, he shall share the destiny of a Śūdra.
One may receive from a Brāhmaṇa all grains except for cooked food; from a Kṣatriya, one may receive cow-peas;
from a Vaiśya, all kinds of grain; but from a Śūdra, no grain at all.
But all that [gift] which is devoid of water and bereft of perfumes and garlands—
whatever has been given among the social classes— a twice-born man should indeed accept it.
Whatever grain has come into the field, or even the mere chaff in the threshing floor, may be taken at all times even from a Śūdra; so Aṅgiras has declared.
Milk that has been given by a pure person to a worthy recipient may be used as a medicinal preparation,
whether with curd or even with milk itself.
Likewise, one should accept [alms] even from Śūdras or from commoners;
or if there is milk or curd in the house of a Śūdra, it may be taken by Brahmins.
One who has withdrawn from worldly life must not drink it, for that is like the food of a Śūdra; nor should one drink it in a fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, by a river, or in the houses of Brahmins.
In a well or likewise in the forest, one may drink milk and curd;
as well as raw meat, curd, ghee, grain, milk, and medicinal herbs.
Molasses, juice, as well as buttermilk, these foods should always be eaten;
likewise, unboiled sour gruel, betel, roasted grain flour, and sesame seeds.
Fruits, oil-cakes, and likewise medicinal herbs—
these pure items are never to be rejected, but should always be accepted.

But when a Brahmin, especially one who is a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), drinks water, eats food, or touches [an impure person] during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) out of ignorance; ||| Ang_2,8.19 |||
If one drinks water [from such a person], one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
if one eats [their food], one must fast for three nights; and if one touches them, bathing is prescribed.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Prohibition of Eating the Food of Śūdras," in the *Āṅgirasa-dharmaśāstra*.
The Ninth Chapter:
Having eaten food during the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) or even during the period of death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) within ten days, [one must perform penance].
A Brahmin, however, should drink the vajra for ten nights for the sake of another Brahmin.
Having eaten the food of a Kṣatriya, one removes [the impurity] in half that time; likewise for a Vaiśya, in five months more; but having eaten the food of a Śūdra, one removes it in three months.

One who has maintained the sacred fires shall observe a three-night penance for eating among members of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes; however, having eaten at the house of a Śrotriya who maintains the Agnihotra fire, he shall observe a five-night penance.
But after that, for those who have bathed, there is no impurity lasting for a month;
nor for any who are consecrated for initiation, nor for kings, nor likewise for those who possess all treasures.
In the case of a sacrificial feast or a gift of cooked food, however, it is censured;
one should perform the Vajra penance for five nights, or the Madhyama penance for six days.
Likewise, one should behave in this same manner for three days regarding other foods unfit for consumption;
except in times of distress, one should subsist on alms while residing in a house where cooked food is available.
One should perform the Vajra penance for ten nights, and in times of distress, one should perform it for three days;
and having eaten the food of any outcasts, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Every month on this day, one should be joyful; otherwise, one would fall [from grace].
Or rather, this [offering] should be performed for a Vedic scholar once every year.
A student of sacred knowledge, an ascetic, one seeking learning, one supporting his teacher, a traveler, and one whose livelihood is exhausted— these six are remembered as those who may beg for alms.
For one who is ill, for one who is poor, for one who has fallen from his family,
or for one who has set out on a journey, the practice of begging for alms is prescribed.
A celibate student bitten by a dog should observe this same practice for three days;
a householder who maintains the *agnihotra* fire, however, should do so for two nights or even one day.
For one bitten above the navel, that same [dose] should be doubled;
for one bitten in the mouth, it should be doubled again, and for one on the head, it should be fourfold.
But from this point forward, when he has bathed and is purified by that very bathing,
then, in all circumstances, he himself becomes a renunciant.
Whether he is one who observes vows or one who does not, a twice-born man bitten by a dog becomes pure immediately upon seeing the fire into which oblations are being offered.
But if a Brahmin woman is bitten by a dog while looking at the Soma, and the Soma is no longer visible, what should the expiation be? (Angulimālīya Sūtra 2.9.15)
One should look toward whichever direction Soma has gone;
that direction, purified by the path of Soma, becomes cleansed by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Rule for Expiation for Eating Forbidden Food," in the *Āṅgirasa-dharmaśāstra*.
Chapter Ten:
One should strike with effort above the staff and cause [the victim] to fall.
A twofold cow-vow is prescribed as his atonement.
The characteristics of the staff:
it should be as thick as a thumb and measure one cubit in length; being fresh and possessed of leaves, it is called a *daṇḍa*. (Angulimālīya-sūtra 2.10.2)
When cattle die due to being confined and so forth, or when they suffer injury from being confined, bound, or yoked,
there exists therein a cause for that death.
One should perform one quarter of the penance for obstructing, two quarters for binding,
three-quarters for confining, and the full penance for causing death.
Cows should not be tied with coconut fiber, nor with hemp, nor with muñja grass, nor even with bark; having bound them, one should remain standing while holding an axe.
One should bind it with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grasses, facing upwards and toward the south;
if there is a snare caught therein or if it is burnt, no expiation is required.
If, however, grief should arise in that regard, what would the expiation be?
Having recited it and brought forth the morning meal, one is liberated from all sins.
Having caused the breaking of a cow's bones, or likewise the cutting off of its tail,
or even the falling off of its horn, one should drink barley gruel for half a month.
When a wound has been treated, an oil massage with the hand should be performed,
and fodder should be provided until the wound has healed.
Likewise, in the case of a fracture of the bones, or similarly a fracture of the horns or the hips,
as long as he lives for six months, no penance is prescribed.
In the case of a broken horn, a fracture of the bone, or likewise the peeling of the skin,
one should drink vajra for ten nights until well-being is restored.
Except for branding and marking, as well as for unyoking the animal,
there is no offense in tethering or binding it in the evening for the purpose of its protection; likewise,
there is no offense in using a mechanical device for the sake of treating cattle or for extracting a dead fetus.
If, despite effort being made, one should fail, no fault is found therein.
One should provide medicine, oil, and food that is beneficial for cows and Brahmins;
for the sake of sustaining the lives of living beings, no expiation is required.
In an elephant, a horse, a tiger, a rhinoceros, a black antelope, a wolf, a lion, a dog, a boar, and even among birds such as peacocks; Ang_2,10.15 //
The Blessed Manu has declared that one should regard a crow, a swan, a vulture, a lapwing, and a wagtail as being exactly like a cow.
Now hear also the rule for that twice-born man who, having grown negligent out of delusion, does not seek an expiation upon returning from his teacher. Ang_2,10.17 //
That which is destroyed by those who lack desire becomes doubled when done out of desire;
furthermore, after committing sins, a human being shall burn with remorse.
Having renounced wealth in one's home, one becomes pure through total renunciation;
or he who, with firm resolve, satisfies the brahmins with abundant riches.
Regarding the atonement for children, the elderly, and women: O noble one, one should prescribe half the penance for women who have committed a sin intentionally;
however, for a man under twelve years of age, he shall indeed be liable for only half the share.
For one who is less than eighty years old, the entire procedure for penance is prescribed; however, for eunuchs, children, the elderly, women, and others of that sort, one should,
after careful consideration, perform only one quarter of it for all of them.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Declaration of Expiations for Violence," in the Dharmaśāstra of Āṅgirasa.
Chapter Eleven:
One who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka) and is a cow-killer shall subsist on barley-gruel (yāvaka).
At the sixth mealtime, his food shall be dry, free from pungent substances and salt.
Having made his dwelling in the forest and being covered by that hide in the cow-pen,
bathing and anointing with cow urine are prescribed for him for two months.
The act of washing the feet should be performed using water alone;
like one observing a vow, he should likewise carry a staff and wear a girdle accompanied by mantras.
One should always follow after the cows and always drink their dust;
one should stand when they stand and walk when they walk.
Having served and paid homage, one should dwell in the heroic posture (vīrāsana) at night;
the wise person should recite the Gomatī, the syllable Om, and the Veda itself.
Whether she is afflicted by illness or accused [of a crime], or threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers;
whether she has fallen or is stuck in the mud—one should liberate her with all one's strength.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first providing protection for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not speak of a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor of a calf drinking. (Angulimālīya Sūtra 2.11.8)
Whoever, by this method, follows cows, is liberated from the sin consisting of cow-slaughter; there is no doubt about this.
One who has well observed his vows should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer all his possessions to those learned in the Vedas.
The merit prescribed for these by Aṅgiras himself—
a destroyer of minor offenses— has been declared by those who know the Dharma and are learned in the Vedas.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Expiation for Killing a Cow," in the *Āṅgirasa-dharmaśāstra*.
Chapter Twelve:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the auspicious rules for expiation.
Having studied, heard, and remembered it, the twice-born indeed attain liberation.
One should always bathe at the three sessions of the day; having bathed once, one should drink milk.
Having bathed in the morning, one should begin the daily recitation of prayers.
One should recite the Sāvitrī or the Vyāhṛtis eight thousand times,
having placed the syllable Oṃ at the beginning, and likewise inserting it within each form.
One who is capable should adopt the hero’s posture (vīrāsana) or indeed any other posture;
his seat should be as if pierced by a thorn, and he should always remain without lying down on his back.
In the absence of cow’s milk, there should be cow’s curd;
in the absence of curd, there should be buttermilk; and in the absence of buttermilk, there should be barley gruel.
Whichever one of these may be appropriate, that he should drink;
the twice-born man should drink barley-gruel mixed with cow’s urine.
This meritorious *kṛcchra* was prescribed by Aṅgiras himself;
it begins with the syllable *praṇava* and is known by the name Vajra.
This expiation is prescribed for those who have committed these sins;
those who are joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) are purified in three years.
Next, the minor offenses (upapātaka) are to be considered, and likewise one should prescribe the appropriate time;
for a Brāhmaṇa is the authority regarding that aforementioned time.
The Brahmins alone are the field; the Brahmins alone are the deity.
By the grace of the Brahmins, the sun shines in the sky.
There is no field equal to a brahmin; there is no fire equal to a brahmin.
There is no ordinance higher than a brahmin, and no destiny superior to a brahmin.
This is true even for those virtuous ones who recite prayers, offer oblations, and practice generosity.
The Brahmin, born from the very womb of Agni, is preeminent today.
It does not overflow, it does not fail, and it never perishes;
that which is offered into the mouth of a Brahmin is superior even to the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Among those who have become like divine barbers, some belong to someone;
all deities reside in the brahmin, and he is the deity of all.
For whoever should desire to propitiate a particular deity,
that person should always satisfy the brahmins with every possible means and effort.

May the dust from the feet of the Brahmins purify me— they who are the cause for attaining all prosperity, the rising banners that destroy the multitude of calamities, and the bridges across the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Kṛcchra and Other Penances," in the *Āṅgirasa-dharmaśāstra*.
This concludes the *Uttarāṅgirasa*,
the *Āṅgirasa-smṛti*.
